The pinafore bodice has wide bretelles composed of guipure lace bordered with bands of crepoline, The Marchioness of Ormonde.—Lady Ormonde, who the lace trimming en the skirt being repeated rarely misses the Cowes regatta week, was in "-former , 4 days a noted rider to hounds, and a daring horse- woman. She is a daughter of the late Duke of,West- minster, and, like all the Grosvenors, is devoted io an open air life, riding, driving and yachting. To those tastes no doubt, she owes the preservation of her youthful appearance, for although a grandmother, she still retains the good looks which Rade her one of the Society beauties of the early seventies. Much of her time is spent on the sea, the Marquis being the Commo- dore of the Royal Yacht Squadron. When in Ireland, Lord and Lady Ormonde reside at Kilkenny Castle. This ancient stronghold is one of the oldest inhabited houses in the British Isles, some of the rooms being almost exactly as they were seven or eight centuries ago. The Memorial to Mrs. Oliphant.—Two years have passed since Mrs. Oliphant died, and her many friends and admirers will be pleased that she is to be worthily honoured by a memorial in St. Giles's Cathedral in Edinburgh. Mrs. Oliphant was the embodiment of the strenuous novelist and journalist. Few writers ever worked harder or more conitantly at high pressure, and it was done mainly to give her sons the advantages of a high-class education. There never was a more strenuous' literary life than hers, carried on too in the face of domostic troubles and bereavement, and the changing tastes of the reading public. The memorial committee has among its members Lord Rosebery, Mr. A. J. Balfour, Mr. William Blackwood, and Mr. J. H. Miller, of 10, Abercromby Place, Edinburgh, the author of the "Literary History of Scotland" is the honorary secre- tary. The Most Popular Authors in our Prisons.—One scarcely knows how popular authors view the fact that their novels are much in demand by the inmates of our prisons. Is it a compliment or the reverse? But, however that may be, it seems that women writers are easily first in prison popularity atieast as regards fiction. ' Accordine to some investigations which'. have bees reported, Miss Braddon is most in request at the prison libraries, her Ishmael" being prime favourite. Next comes " Ouida " whose "Under two flags" and "Strathmore," are in continuous demand, and third on 4 the list is Edna Lyall. But it seems there are books more sought after by prisoners than any of the works of fiction writers of the present and past generations. The new Oriental satins are fairly moderate in price, they clean well and moreover emerge trium- phantly from a visit to the dyer. Forthcoming Tailor Modes.—When early autumn arrives, violet will be the most popular colour, and next on the list will come a certain shade of red purple. which is likely to prove the more generally becoming. The skirt that just escapes the ground will be the one built by leading tailors for morning wear, walking and travelling, and coats are to be of three- quarter length. Like so many of our modes however, the short skirt and long coat idea is one suited only to the very tail and slender,and despite the fact that short coats will be considered out of date, they will prove the wiser choice for those of us less favoured by Nature. The Matutinal meal.—The national belief in "a thorough good breakfast " is so well established that little heed is paid 'to suggested reforms of the matutinal meal. French people start the day on a roll and coffee, but in this country max would go in fear of a break- down during the morning on such a trifle. The foreign system of getting through the morning's work before the mid-day meal is, without doubt, the best, but it is opposed to our long-established theory of a substaatial breakfast, and is not convenient to our accustomed habits. It is unfortunately true that simple cooking is not so well understood in this country as it is in France and Germany, and there is a monotony about our break- fast dishes which is in striking contrast to the French dejvcner. Then our breakfast is not the social meal it is in France. it is generally hurriedly prepared and scrambled through, the idea being to consume as much as possible in the shortest space of time. It is our way, and it is to be feared that all the recommendations of the Food Reformers "ill not induce us to alter it.

ATIE VERDICT OF THE HEART.
,By CHARLES GARVICE,
Author di "Her Heart's Desire," "In Cupid's Chains," "Just a Girl," "Nance," "The Out- cast of the Family," "A Coronet of Shame," eso.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: The story opens in Australia, where Ralph Farringdon is present at the deathbed of his mother. They are poor, and she has been deserted by her husband, Ralph's step-father. With almost her last breath, she tells Ralph of papers in her box which are of importance to him. Her words are overheard by a man with the appearance of a tramp, who steals into the house and abstracts the 'contents of the box. The scene then changes to 'Lynne Court, where Lord Lynborough, aged and in failing health,, is in residence, his beautiful niece, Veronica Denby, ruling the household as chateleine. One day the Earl sends for Veronica and informs her that it is his intention to leave her by will his whole fortune, his nephew, Talbot Denby, suc- ceeding only to the title and the entailed estates. He asks if she will accept the condition that she wed only a man of title. Veronica, who is as proud as she is fair, and who has known grinding poverty during her father's life, readily consents. Riding afterwards on the neighbouring moor she is struck with the gallant act of a young stranger, who snatches a puppy from under her horse's feet, receiving some slight injury in consequence. He refuses pecuniary reward, but asks to be taken on as one of the Earl's gamekeepers. Lord Lynborough, coming up in his carriage, refers the applicant to his head man. The stranger, who gives the name of Ralph Farringdon, and says he has come from Australia, obtains the coveted job. The reader is now taken to London, and Talbot Denby is intro- duced—a rising young Conservative M.P., am- bitious, talented, but a confirmed gambler of the worst type. Veronica sees Ralph Farringdon fishing in the park stream, and is at once attracted and irritated by the ease of his manner towards her, which is not that of a dependant. He shews her how to throw the line, and in her attempts she gets the hook fixed in her wrist. Ralph cuts it out, and applies his lips to the wound to draw out any possible poison. At that moment, Talbot Denby—who has been informed of the Earl's testamentary resplve, and hence wishes to marry Veronica—comes 'upon the pair.

You look strong—a keeper's life is a hard one at the Court, for there are plenty of poachers." "So I am aware," said Ralph. "I'm con- tinually finding snares, and I fancy that some men have been trying the woods ever...since I came."

The steward seemed to be still listening to a far-away echo, and he nodded his head absently, while his eyes rested on the handsome face. "You don't know these parts at all, then ? " he said. "Not till you came? No? Of course not, of course not. I hope you like your situation ? "
"Yes, thanks," said Ralph; "that is, fairly well."

"Nothing to complain of ? "asked the steward, quickly. You live with Mr. Burchett ? You get on with him? He's—he's not easy to get on with. No, no; but he has had a great deal to try him. He has told you, perhaps ? " he added, with a quick glance at Ralph. "No," said Ralph. "That is "—remembering Mr. Burchett's words just now—"no, he has not told me, though I gathered that he had had some trial."
"A terrible one," said the steward absently. "So terrible a one that he is entitled to your forbearance, Farringdon. Will you remember that ? "

"I will," said Ralph; "though up to the present Mr. Burehett has been most kind to me. He's not what you could call sociable or very cheerful"--with a smile—"but I'm used to all sorts a men out there in the wilds, you know, sir.".

The steward nodded. "Will you have a glass of wine ? " he said almost abruptly; and without waiting for a reply, he got a decanter of sherry, and pouring out a glass watched Ralph, as he drank it, so intently that he seemed., lost and quite absorbed in the process. Ralph put the glass down. "No message— answer, I suppose, sir ? " he said.
"No no," said Mr. Whetstone rousinc,

self with a little start. "I will write lo his lordship. Er—er —good-day." He sank into his chair, but looked round presently. "You'd better come up to me now and again," he said. "Of course, I leave everything concerning the game to Mr. Burchett, but I like to know from time to time how things go on." "Certainly," said Ralph. "Good-day, sir." He had got halfway down the passage when he remembered the weir, and the weeds in the South pool, and he went back quickly. "I beg your pardon," he said, apologetically, for the steward was bending over a small minia- ture in an open case which lay on the desk before him, and which certainly had not been there when Ralph left the room.
The steward covered the miniature with a swift movement of his hand and looked round with a startled expression. "Oh, it's yo! , What is it? "he stammered.
Ralph delivered himself of the object of his return, and Mr. Whetstone, after listening absently, dismissed him with a nod. "I'll see to it—yes, yes ! " he said. day!"
"Good-

I Ralph, favourably impressed Iby the gentle I I manner of the old man, and the kindness with/ I which he had treated him, was going back to the hut by the way he came, when he remembered I that he had to get some wire in the village, and I he struck into the road.

He had not gone far when he caught sight of a man crouching amongst the bracken in the woods a few paces from the open fence. Ralph walked on quietly,and, suddenly vaulting the paling, laid his hand on the man's shoulder.
He sprang to his feet and presented to Ralph an exceedingly ugly and evil-looking face, rendered all the more unprepossessing by a scowl, half-fearful, half-defiant.
"What are you doing here ? "demanded Ralph; though he could give a pretty shrewd guess, for the place swarmed with rabbits, and rabbits are tempting things to a hungry tramp.

Ralph's quick eyes saw that the man's right hand held a useful, and businesslike stick, and that his left was wrapped in a dirty and blood- stained bandage. "What gm I doin' ere F" retorted the man. "What d'ye s'pose I'm doin'? I was goin' to 'ave a doss, that was what I was doin'." "Well, I'm sorry to disturb you," said Ralph, gravely, but good-humouredly enough, "but you're trespassing; find besides, you must not go to sleep here. 'You'd snore, perhaps, and disturb the rabbits."

"Ho!" said the man, with a sneer. "And who may you be? You might own the belly place for the airs you give yourself." "No, I don't own it, worse luck," said Ralph, who was trying to place the man • for, though he looked a tramp, he was a little different to those Ralph was acquainted with in England. This man had rather a foreign—ah, yes, that was it, Ralph jumped to the conclusion—a Colonial touch. 'l'm only one of the men who look after the bunnies, see ? " _ _ _

"Oh, a kind of peeler," said the man. "Well, why don't you wear the proper uniform? And what do you mean by swaggering along as if you was lord of all you survey? Come to that, who does own this place, mister ? " "Lord Lynborough," replied Ralph, rather curtly. "And now, if you've asked all the questions you want to, perhaps you'll get the other—the right—side of the fence." The man snorted and looked Ralph up and down. "Haven't got a pipe of 'baeca about you, I suppose ? " he said, sullenly. Ralph took out his pouch. It is an appeal a man can rarely resist. "Help yourself," ho said.

The man took the pouch and was filling his pipe groedily, when a dog-cart came down the road. Ralph looked up,and saw that it was one from the Court, and that the gentleman seated beside the groom was Mr. Talbot Denby, evidently on his way to the station. The tramp looked up also. The pouch was suddenly crushed in his hand, and, slipping behind a tree, the man leant forward and stared 31 Talbot Denby with so strange an expression, one so full of amazement and malignity, that Ralph was staggered. "Who---who's that ?" he asked, hoarsely, his bandaged hand laid on Ralph's with as much al a clutch as its condition would allow. "Who is it ? Quick! He'll be past! Tell me his name, hang you!" "Keep a civil tongue in your head, my friend," said Ralph, ,sternly, "and get over thi.t -fence. I've had about enough of you." The dog-cart was just abreast of them and the man, hissing warningly and shrinking further behind the tree, glared at Talbot until he had passed. Thep he drew his bandaged hand aerdss his face as if to wipe away the sweat which had started on it, and turned' to Ralph with a flickering, deprecating leer. "Beg pardin, mate," he said. "I only thought as I'd seen the genel'man afore. But I see I was mistook. Anybody can be mistook, can't they ?" he whined. "There ain't no 'arm in lsking you who the swell is, is there ?" "He is Mr. Talbot Denby, Lord Lynborough's nephew and heir," said Ralf. as the quickest way of getting rid of the man. "I'll trouble you fog my pouch. Thanks. And now---" "lOgrit, right you are, guy' nor," said the man. "I'm much obliged to you for the 'bacea, and—your kind answers to my enkwiries; very much obliged!" Ralph watched him as he went down the road, ind saw him presently turn his evil and still working face to gaze after the departing dog- cart, his stout clay pipe clenched so tightly between his bloated lips that the yellow fangs were exposed like those of a savage cur, _

div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
- . - Water in which rice has been boiled may be used fOr starching old lace, 'choice i:aaid- kerchiefs, eta. It gives a soft and daiilty stiffness which adds a charm to the appear- ance.
Hot water used both internally and - exter- nally is highly recommended b2,'• medical men as a cure for insomnia. - Bathing the feet in hot water is said to be particularly efficacious.

If moths are in a carpet turn it over and iron on the wrong side with a good het flat iron. Then sprinkle the floor with tuipen- tine, rub it well in, and 'turn the carpet .back. Repeat the treatment two or three times.
Finger-marks on woodwork can be • easily removed by rubbing them with a cloth dipped in paraffin oil. Wipe off with a cloth wrung out in hot water, and rub dry with another cloth.

Bamboo furniture may be cleaned with a small brush dipped in warm water and salt. The salt prevents the bamboo from turning yellow, and washing ft,_ makes it look bright. Rub it very dry with Rbft cloths, and the result will, be most satisfactory.

Baked Cup Aiddings.—Beat two eggs very lightly, add two teacupfuls of niilk, two cup- fuls of flour, and ane teaspoonful of baking powder. Beat all together for ten minutes, place in small greased cups, and bake in a very quick oven. Serve with sweet sauce.
Linoleum is a much better covering for a, kitchen floor than ordinary oilcloth. The
initial expense may be a litle greater, but Linoleum always looks fresh and clean if pro- perly cared for, and wears considerably Longer than oilcloth.

When soot falls on carpet do not attempt to sweep it, or thd'result will be an ineradic- able smear. Dry some salt •thoroughly, and sprinkle it over the soot. Then sweep, and no trace of the soot will remain.

To analyse well water, put a small pinch of permanganate of potash into a wineglassful of water, do not stir it, but just observe the Colour; if of a dull claret or maroon, be sure it is impregnated—the worse the colour the worse the danger.

One of the best disinfectants for a sponge that has been allowed to get into a bad con- dition is to wash it in a strong Solution of washing soda, after which it should be rinsed with a weak solution of hydrochloric acid.,

The creases can be taken out of velvet and the pile raised by drawing it across a hot iron on which a wet cloth has been spread. . if there are pin-marks over which the , pile re- fuses to rise, brush it up with) a stiff brush and steam it, repeating the operation several times.

Oatmeal Biscuits. Mix .together half a pound of flour, quarter of a pound of oat- meal, and two ounces of sugar. Stir into this two ounces of 'melted butter or dripping and one well-beaten egg. Knead the dough thoroughly and, if necessary, add a little milk. Roll out on a floured board, cut into squares, and bake on a. greased tin.

Coral ornaments should be put in a pan ef boiling water with some small pieces of white soap and soda. The water shoulthen be boiled for a few minutes. when the orna- ments can be removed, rinsed in clean water, .and left 'until dry. They should then be polished carefully with a clean chamois leather.

When meat is frozen, it should be soaked. in cold water until all the frost is extracted, and then be cooked in the usual way. if tins is not done and the frost remains in,. the joint will be found most difficult to cook. Vegetables that are frozen must, when they have been prepared for cooking, be placed for some little time in .plenty of salted, cold water to cover them.

Irish Hashed Mutton.--frry slices of cold mutton in dripping till lightly browned and hot. Have a border of mashed 'potatoes on a hot dish and brown it before the fire. Have ready some good onion • sauce, in which chopped parsley ,is mixed. Stir this into the moat and pile in the centre of the potato. Scatter chopped capers or pickles. over, and serve very hot.

If glazed tiles are spotted, wash them with lemon juice, leave them for a quarter of. an hour, and finally rub them with a soft cloth. Tiles filould not be washed, but only .rubbed with a (laMp cloth, and then polished with shim milk and Water. Perhaps a rag on which a little paraffin has been sprinkled is the best of all polishers; but it • should be usod before a fire is lit in the grate.

Curry Soup.—Chop an onion and a carrot finely and fry in butter until well browned. Then add a chopped apple, a tablespoonful of curry powder, and an ounce of flour. Stir well over the fire, and when hot add some good fish. stock, work wdll -until the mixture boils, then withdraw to ihe side of the stove and • simmer for an hour. Strain, add any remains of cold boiled fish—divided into small pieces—and serve with boiled rice.

Stuffed Potatoes.—Choose some nice large potatoes and bake them; when quite done, cut off an end and scoop out some of the Fill( up the hollow with sonic cold meat chopped finely, seasoied with chopped herbs, parsley, popper and salt, moistened with a little run butter. Make the whole into a paste with some gravy. With the aid- of a little white of egg stick the end on again and bake for five to ten .minutes. Serve hot.

Rhubarb Tarts.—Line some patty pan tins with short crnst. • Put into each some pink rhubarb cut small ; add sugar, a little ginger, and a squeeze of lemon, or a little grated rind. Cover with paste, like mince-pies. Bat up the white of .an egg. to a froth. Put a little over each pie, sift castor sugar on, and bake.

To clean sponges, place a pennyworth of salts of lemon in a quart of boiling water and soak the sponge in it. After an hour rinse thoroughly in warm water or drop the spolige into water in which 'a large lump of soda has been. dissolved, afterwards boiling slowly. Rinse thoroughly in cold water, and .place in the sun until dry.

A piano is as sensitive to cold and heat as an invalid, so it must not be put too near a fire,, or the wood is drawn by the heat. Never leave it near an open window. if it is raining, or in a damp room, as this .will rust the wires and mould the inside. Such an instrument should not be put close to a wall; or the sound will be deadened, and it should, .be kept closed when not in use. The keys should be dusted daily with an old silk hand- kerchief, but, they should never be washed when they are soiled or the ivory will be dis- coloured. If they become yellow from neglect rub them well with lemon-juice and a little whiting, and when it is dry brush it off, Ira do not let the dust fall between the keys.
To clean a white felt hat' brush it over carefully with a paste made of arrowroot or magnesia, mixed well with cold water, allow it to dry. thoroughly, th9n. brush it off..
_ - Heat a lemon thoroughly before 8.4.-teezing it, and you will obtain nearly double quantity of juice that would be obtaii:ed A were not heated.

div.head: SALE OF HACKNEYS AT WALTON.
div.p: SALE OF HACKNEYS AT WALTON.

£2,375 Realised. Sir Gilbert Greenall held a sale of pedigree hackney and hackney pony marbs and foals, two and three year old fillies, harness mud, &c., at his residence, Walton Hall, near Warrington, on Wednesday. Mr. W. Baja- bridge conducted the sale. The fifty-two animals sold fetched £2,375. They were all from celebrated families and many of the brood mares had won at London and other principal shows. The best price realised was 195 guineas for Rosarene, by Rosador, dam Elegance, the London champion in 1901 and 1902. Golden Ethel, by Goldfinder VI., dam Lady Ethel, one of the best pony brood mares in England, went for 155 guineas. The chief sales and purchasers were as follows (the prices given represent guineas) : Hackney Brood Mares and Foals.—Rosarene, I\Tr. Benson, Upper Gatton Park, 195: Rosarene's colt foal, Mr. Ferguson, Macclesfield, 46 ; Dorothy Burton, Mr. M`Meeken, Glasgow, 95; Terrington's Starlight's filly foal, Mr. Macaulay, Nebraska, 54; Terrington Comely, Mr. Fogg, Little Lever, 46; Florence, Mr. M`Meeken, 48. Pony Brood Mares and Foals.—Golden Ethel, Mr. M`Meeken' 155; Golden Ethel's colt foal, Mr. Gemmel!, Ayr, 40; Tissington Joan Crompton Mr. J. Jones, Whitegate, Wrexham, 77; Tissington Crompton, Halo, Mr. Harrop,, Oldham, 105 Tsssington Merrielees, Mr. Smith, Crank, St. Helens, 60; Gold Foil, Mr. Le Marcbant, Bromley, Kent, 70. Harness Mares.—Terrington Modiste, Mr. Salmon, 68; Bold Clara, Mr. Ainsworth, Waterloo, 95. Three-year-old Fillies.—Terrington Britannia, Mr. J. Jones, 38 ; Lakes Kate, Mr. Kennedy, Dublin, 43.

div.head: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

Corporation and Electricity Supply. • The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council was held-on Wednesday at Bewsey Chambers, Mr. R. Forshaw presided, and amongst those present were :—Messrs. A. Brooks, G. Mather, W. Houghton, W. Furness. W. Stanter, P. Longton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor), F. W. Kerfoot (inspector), hud Dr. Sephton (medical officer). THE CORPORATION'S ELECTRICITY PROPOSALS.

1111,1 The Clerk read a letter from the Town Clerk of Warrington with reference to the proposal of the Corporation to apply for a provisional order to supply electricity in the area of the Rural Council as follows: "This order has not yet been printed and much will depend upon the attitude taken by the districts affected whether the application is proceeded with. I will keep your letter before me with a view to a copy of the order being forwarded to you when in print." A letter was also read front Mr. John Fairclongh, clerk to , the Burtonwood Parish Codncil, asking the District Council to oppose the Provisional Order being granted. Mr. BROOKS said they were not going to show their attitude until they knew what the order was. He would propose that they let the Corpor‘tion know that they would oppose any attempt for them to get a general order giving them the monopoly for the supply of electricity in their districts. Mr. G. MATHER seconded. The CLERK: I take it that pending the receipt of a copy of the Order, the Council would oppose the Pro- visional Order. Mr. BROOKS: Yes. The resolution was carried. ASYLUM DRAINAGE._

. The CLERK read a letter from Mr. J. Stanley Fran- comb, Clerk to the Committee of Visitors of the Winwick Asylum, asking the permission of the Council to the taking of the effluent drain from the asylum sewage beds along Mill-lane. Mr. BROOKS said that if it.was a matter of urgency a small committee, with the officials, could be appointed to consider the matter, and be authorised to give permission if they thought it was desirable. Mr. FURNESS said tbe Council ought to be satisfied that it was not the intention of the Asylum authorities to further pollute the brook. Messrs. Furness, Longton, the Surveyor, and the Inspector were appointed to go into the matter. WINWICK ASYLUM ASSESSMENT. - -

The CLERK said had attended a meeting of the County Rating Committee at the Town Hall, Man- chester, and he intimated to them that they should put £3,000 more on the Winwick Asylum Assessment. instead of being £7OOO it would .be £lO,OOO for rating purposes. Several representatives from the Asylum were there, and said they would oppose it if it went forwarcl. They increased it by £1,500 for county pur- noses, but he (the Clerk)would certainly go in for £3OOO more. MEDICAL OFFICERS' REPORT. Dr. SEPIITON reported that during the month there had been 31 births and 35 deaths. The death-rate from all, causes was equal to 34 per thousand as against 27, the average of the last three months, and 22 for the corresponding period of last year. The death-rate. from zymotic diseases (7 principal) was 6.8 per thousand, as against '6, the average rate of the last three months,and nil the corresponding month of last year. Twenty deaths occurred in the County Asylum at Winwick, and the death-rate proper for the district was equal to 14.0 per thousand. At the time for re-opening the schools at Burtonwood the epidemic of measles was still pro- gressing and he advised the managers to postpone the opening until after the holidays. SPITTLE BRIDGE. •

The SURVEYOR r;;;it-e—d thethe had examined Spittle Bridge and was of opinion that it would be perfectly, safe for many years to come if the northerly end were concreted for about 7 feet from the face of the arch and the abutment shored up. The cost of 'this should not he more than about £4O, but it was difficult to foresee exactly what might happen in disturbing new work. A discussion ensued with reference to property that I would have to be acquired and it was recommended that the Surveyor should draw a new line to exclude certain property.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 10, 1907.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 10, 1907.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.)

"Ah ! Number Nine," said he, glancing at fay disc which I produced, but asking no other credential. "Here is your badge; kindly sigr the— Yes, that is right. Deputy? Just so. Now, if you will draw a lot-- What is it Four? Then you are a fixed star. and that table over by the window is yours. In ."—and he drew out his watch, an exceedingly handsome plait gold hunter—"seven minutes we shall begin, ani here, in good time, comes our twelfth member.' With a nod I passed on to the middle of thc room and looked about me. Nine or ten mer were grouped here and there in twos or threes, chatting and laughing. I knew none personally, but more than one were dimly familiar througl the medium of the illustrated press as artist, at a writer of books that sold, or, like the president himself, Its counsel in some case which had set the ears of the public itching. Scattered about the room were six tables, each with two piquet packs standing onlicoring cards. From the nearest group a man turned toward* me with cordial. outstretched hand. "I wonder if I would be quite honest if l wished you good luck ? " "Perfect honesty," replied I, "would dis- rupt any society; not even sweet. charity would stand against it." "Ah ! " said he, "you are cynical. have lost last week!" "Lost ? " returned I. "How lost? "Twere good you do so much for charity ! ' " "Fudge ! " he answered; "and Portia knew it was fudge when she said it. It is true I am only a miserable stop-gap deputy, here on sufferance, but I am here because it amuses me to see— But there goes the president's bell. What is your table number? Four? Then you are a fixture for the night and my last antagonist, since I have drawn five and must revolve the circle. We meet again three hours hence!" To describe the varying fortunes of the night is unnecessary. It is enough to say that the involuntary almoner of the club for the night was the man who had introduced himself as ' Number Five.
You must

"May the recording angel set it to my credit! said he, with a shrug, as he reckoned up the score. "The points against me are two hundred and sixty-five, which, translated into hard coin, is six pounds twelve shillings and six- pence." From his purse he produced a five-pound note, into which he folded two gold coins and a half- crown. "Well, gentleman' let us hope it will do more good in the world than my nine pounds eleven this day fortnight. They fell a prey to a mother of nine who the week before had been a blind father of five. That is the beauty of the system." Ten minutes later we left the hotel together, and turning into the Strand strolled towards Trafalgar-square. "Your first experience ? " said he. "And probably my last." He shook his head as he paused to light * cigarette. "Not if you can help it. It's a foolish business I grant, and a trifle contemptible that a dozen sane men should squander four hours in order that one of their number should fling good money down the gutter; for nine times in ten that's what it means. Foolish and contemptible, and yet come now, be honest—you liked the evening?" "Well, it was novel, and the company—" "Thank you—was mixed? But company is like a salad, and all the better for a mixture. If it were all white of egg it .would be very insipid; a touch of garlic, now, to flavour the vinegar, adds-- What's that?"

At that dead hour of the night there was com- paratively little life astir, and a quick thud of hoofs racing past St. Martin's Church compelled attention as twelve hours earlier a runaway might have done. We had crossed to the angle of the square and pausing turned to look northward. A hansom was tearing down the slope at a break- neck pace, but as it neared us its occupant flung back the folding apron and, rising, waved his hand urgently over the roof of the cab. Leaning back in his perch the driver reined up his horse, curving inward as he did so alongside the pavel ment where we stood, and his fare, a young fellow of six or eight and twenty, leaped out. A heavy overcoat thrown back shewed him to be in evening dress, and as he came towards us the dulness of a crush hat caught my eye. So assured was his manner that I assumed he had found a friend, and involuntarily turned to my companion for confirmation. But apparently the same thought was in his mind also, for in the dimness of the lamp I saw him shoot a question- ing glance at me, even as I at him, and then back at the newcomer.
"I hardly know how to explain myself," he began. _

But my fellow-deputy. hastily interrupted the apology, "Explanation?" he cried. ,"No, no explana- tions are ruinous; where would the best of us be if we had to explain ourselves! Come to the point. but never mind the whys and wherefores:" "That's all very well," said the other; "but when a man has to ask a favour of strangers--" "Ask away. There's nothing easier than asking in this world--unless it's refusing." The cab had slightly overshot us, and now the driver pulled his horse back .a pace or two. . -"I want to get home, guv'nor," said he, leaning aslant from his perch. "Suppoae you pay pe first and do your palaverin' afterwards." The newcomer shrugged his shoulders with a little deprecatory wave of the hands. "Jehu Ins hit the blot, gentlemen. I owe him half-a- crown, and have not a penny piece in my pockets. It was only as I drove away from Blackford'* that I found--"

"Blackford'e ? " interrupted my companion— "Blackford's, the gambling hell ?" "I suppose you might call it that." "I suppose I might," repeated the other, drily. "You are not the first man.,who has come away with empty pockets from Blackford's, though, to do the rest of Your tribe justice; I think they could mostly pay their cabs." - . A silence followed, broken at last by the stranger. "My peculiar difficulty is that—because of what passed to-night—l have vowed never to accept a loan--" _

"Then by George! it's charity," broke in my friend. 'My dear fellow, why didnt you say so at once? Here, you are." Out of his vest pocket he • fished the little rolledrup • bundle of volley and pushed it into the other man's hand. 'nou have relieved me of a serious difficulty. A fit object for the blessings of charity is exactly what I'm searching for. Pay, cabby, and let us stroll on. "But--"

"But--but—but—you're not the only man ‘vho t:: vowed vows! Charity," he went on, pom- pously, "has its responsibilities as well as its privileges. It's take that—or do without." [landing the cabman the piece of silver the s`r.mger ?ollowed-us slowly, a puzzled look on his face, as well there might be. "Of course, I am very gratefAl," he began. - "Gratitude! r said I, who, having done nothing for him, could afford to be cynical--"you know the proverb? though really I don't know what more you could expect." : "And it's a true one, for what I want is a favour to come, and a more serious one than the last. At Blackford's to-night I borrowed from a man I knew but.. slightly, played with the borrowed money, and. lost; borrowed again, and attain lost. Later, playing ecart6 with the same .0 man I saw him cheat most flagrantly, and it flashed upon me that all the time I had been losing he stood at my elbow, and could have signalled 'my opponent. On the spur of the moment I accused him--"
"Fie—fie!" said my companion. "Borrow money from a man who ia almost a stranger and then call him a swindler. Was that well done ? "

"I know I was wrong," replied the other, humbly; "but this Schrenck angered me, his cheating was almost ostentatious, and I forgot myself. ‘Sehrenck ? " Pausing as he spoke, my friend laid his hand on the gamester's shoulder, and under the flare of a lamp the two stood facing. "This Schrenck, who lends money to half- strangers—not a Continental practice—and then Cheats them is he an Austrian ? " "Yes, I believe so. He challenged me on the spot—of course denying the charge—and, having r taken \ his money,. how could I refuse to meet I him ? "
"Sehrenek, the Vienna 9naitre d' esc;inie—the first .swordsman in Europe! My friend, my friend, whose path do you bledk, that they seek Lo murder you?" "I am-----"

"Never mind that. Who you are matters nothing to us. You are a man, but if Sehrenelc have his will of you for five minutes you will be lint. the memory of a mnn, and no more • mm-bh good names would do you or us then. When do you meet him ?" "Now, at Daly's Shooting Gallery:" "Daly's—at this hour? How comes Daly's open at two in the morning?"

"That I don't know. it was Schrenbk wno named the place, and swore that after such a public insult we must meet at once." "You must meet at once! Of course. Schrenck overlooks your hand and you lose; Schrenck lends you money to pay your debts; Schrenck, as clever at cards as he is with the rapier, cheats so clumsily that you find him out and denounce him; Schrenck has Daly's Gallery open and lit up at two in the morning—and it all seems to you the easy matter of course, slipping of cir- cumstance into cireumstance with no forethought, no sinister intent behind it? Sir, it's murder— frank callous, premeditated murder, and you may thank Heaven you had not so much as a cab fare in your pocket., For once an empty purse has saved a life."

"If it has saved it!" answered the other, gloomily. "I understand the plot now, and yet I must meet this fellow. If I were out of the way, my cousin-" "That is none of our business. It is enough that you know who stands in the shadow behind Schrenck, guiding Schrenck's hand. Yes, you must meet him. That is essential. He would whisper a dozen lying tales if you did not, tales that., after your borrowings you would find it hard to disprove, and there are times when a lie can kill almost as surely as a rapier. But I think I can promise you it will all end in a bout of the foils.

Passing through Leicester-square we turned down an alley between tall houses. The place was new to me, but both of my companions were evidently-familiar with their surroundings, for midway down the alley they halted at a door sunk in a blank wall. It was .unlocked and opened at a touch. Crossing a small square yard we went up four or five steps, at the head of which was another open door. "Go. you in front," said my friend; "I will follow last, and remember that from this on your honour is in our hands. Take"my word for it, it will be safe, and you also." The other nodded, and, I following, crossed a hall which served as a kind of vestibule to the gallery beyond. This latter was in shadow at the ends, but the centre was-lit by a Bare of gas bright enough to light a dozen souls out of the world. Full in the glare three men were stand- ing, and ,on a narrow table drawn on one side my eyes caught the glint of steel. .The readiness was complete in all details. A yard or, two inside the gallery our principal paused. "That is Schrenck," he said; "and yes, by Jove! you are right. The fellow with him is the man who--'

"Won the money which Schrenck lent you. Of course; but it shows how sure the scoundrel is of you that he dares to bring him here. You may ask questions as to why men who were strangers at Blackford's are here together, but v* i who s to answer them I And if they are left unanswered you cannot turn on your heel and go. You have a reputation to save—but that is our affair."

Putting us quietly aside he stepped to the front, and sauntered slowly down the gallery. "Good-morning, Herr Schrenck ! " he cried, pleasantly, and- with an airy wave of his hands. "No, no; no names if you please; it is enough that here we are gentlemen who—er—know one another, and the formality of a name is unneces- sary. Ido not even ask to be introduced to either of your friends, pray understand that." At the sound 9f his voice I saw the fencing- master start and shoot a sudden word or two across his shoulder at the man who stood nearest him; but beyond a bow, lower than seemed reasonable, he made. no reply.. "I think," went on the deputy charity corn- missioner—"l think this little affair will be easily settled. I see you have the rapiers laid out? Really, it is very convenient that Daly's should be so opportunely open at this hour of the morning, that Daly himself a very honest fellow—should be absent, and that duelling rapiers should be so accom- modatingly ready I It does credit to your inspira- tion, your—er—spirit of prophecy. I'll wager there is not another man in London, except your friends there, who forecasted that Daly's would be wanted for such a purpose at this dismal hour, and yet, here is all prepared, as if it had been arranged beforehand by a loving forethought—a loving forethought," he added, smiling apprecia- tion ; then, after the briefest pause went on, swiftly: "Do you know what they do to murderers in this country, Herr Schrenck ? They hang them, and, by Heavens ! sir, if ill comes of this night's plotting, hang you shall, with your two friends to keep you company. Accessories before the fact is what we call them in England, gentle- men, but we hang them all the same. Now that you are warned we may proceed to our sword play. The tragedy has become a farce, but, nevertheless, it must be played to the fall of the curtain. Eh, Schrenck ? Your reputation would suffer, you know, your good name would be blasted, you could never look your —er—patron' in the face if you did not meet this gentleman!" Going to the table he lifted the two rapiers and examined them closely.

"Honest enough," he said, testing their swing and balance. "Choose your weapons, gentlemen," he went on, flinging them back upon the table. Only once did Schrenck speak—it was when, ten seconds after, as the men faced one another, he sent our friend's sword clattering agaiqst the roof with a peculiar viciousness. "You see," said he, saluting, and throwing aside his own blade. "You see I could have done it, and I would!" "For once," said my fellow-deputy, as we said good-night at the corner of the Haymarket—"for once that tomfoolery of a charity club has done some good in the world." '
[THE END.]
Ling but St,

div.head: MAN WITHOUT A PURSE.
div.p: THE MAN WITHOUT A PURSE.
1 By HAMILTON DRUMMOND, Author of "For The Religion," "A Man of His Age," King's Pawn," "The Seven Houses," : "On Behalf of the Firm," "Room Five," &e.

Until one evening in October I had never so much as *heard of the Charity Club, and, to prevent misapprehension, let me say at once that, in spite of its name, it is neither a Dorca.r. Society nor a soup kitchen. •My introduction to it came about in this way. As I dressed, preliminary to hunting up a solitary dinner at my club, the following note was brought to me from Calthorpe. You may have heard of Calthorpe? Twenty years or so ago he went in for doing out-of-the-way things as if he liked them. A man who cannot be great can often .be notorious, and so Calthorpe took to exploring hinterlands that nobody owned or wanted to own; to crossing Manchuria in dirt, discomfort, and a pigtail; Co sounding for ocean chasms' and being supremely proud of a half- fa hornbeyond the depth the last man had struck— all highly scientific and 'entirely valueless; but, being a bachelor with eight thousand a-year, he had, I suppose, the right to spend his income and his time as he pleased. Somehow or other, being Calthorpe, he got value for his money. This was his letter:

"My dear Boy, —I have a worry—and the gout. Come across to-night and relieve me of the one if you can ; as to the other, Belas says--but never mind what Belas says, come over and see me, there's a good fellow. —Ever yours, T. CA ITHORPE.

It chanced I had no engagement that. night, and as he still has the eight thousand a-year I went across after dinner to -the hotel where he roomed and looked him up. He was on the sofa nursing a leg as big as a mummy with elephantiasis. "Good boy, Winslow!" ,he cried. "I knew you would come. No, no, you fool! don't touch me, I'm red-hot to the linger-tips ! " "I'm sorry," I began. 'Oh, this is nothing!" he went on, hastily, "a few days on the sofa, nothing more; anyhow, if Belas can't cure it I don't suppose you can. But the mind's diseased, my boy, and that is where you can help. I have a worry, and it aggravates this—this--" and he slid off into what might have been Thibetan, Finxiish, or East- African Portuguese, so far as the words went, but was none the less perfectly comprehensible as the equivalent of a bargee's opinions of a newly-created black eye. "Have you to-morrow night free ? " he asked when the steam had at last blown off.

"Urn---" I began, cautiously, for if it was to he spent listening to polyglot objurations I rather thoughtll had an engagement that could not possibly be put off. Calthorpe, confound him, quite understood the cause of my reticence, for he grinned wickedly. That is the worst of these beggars who travel amongst strange folk. The ease with which they read a man's face is perfectly indecent. "No," he said, still grinning; no, not with me. You're a good fellow, Winslow, but I don'l think either of us could stand the other for a whole evening. At least, I know one of us whc couldn't. I'm glad you're not engaged, for nox:, you'll be able to do me a kindness—that is, if you can play piquet, as of course you can ? " "I've seen the game played," I answered, still cautiously—l am suspicious of Calthorpe when he is too civil—"but I'm not an expert, and piquet--you lenow what I mean? It's a game at which a man might soon drop--" "That is all right; we don't play for money." "Oh,.you don't, don't you? Then what do you play for?" "Charity, my boy, charity."

"Charity? echoed, feebly. Soinehow, I had always understood that Calthorpe found a very personal use for his whole eight thousand a-year, to the very last sixpence, and, anyhow, it seethed a mad idea. "You play for charity? Play piquet for charity? How in the world do you do that ? "

"Twelve of us meet each weelt at the Monopole Hotel in Craven-street for eight months in the year. Whoever • cannot attend must provide a substitute and you see how it is with me? I'm greatly obliged to you, Winslow, for taking my place." _
.." Who are the other men ?" I asked. "Do I know them ? "

But Calthorpe shook his head. 'f'We never mention names," he said. "The man you play with may be your bootmaker or the premier Duke in England. Unless you know him socially else- where you meet as strangers, except within the four walls of the club-room. We are known by our numbers."
"Your numbers ? " lam afraid my echo was again a feeble one. It sounded like prize beasts in a cattle show.

"Yes. Mine is on the mantelshelf, if you don't mind looking." Lying conspicuously to the forefront was an ivory disc of about the diameter of a five-shilling piece. Number nine was stamped upon it, and above the number a slit was punched, through which ran a loop of crimson ribbon. "Yes," went on Calthorpe, as I shewed him the token, "that is it. Put it.in your pocket, will you, and I'll tell you what to do. You know the Monopole? No! Well, it's easily found. Shew the number to the hall-porter, and he will tell you in which room the club is meeting. Just inside the door you will find, on a small table, a book ruled with twelve horizontal spaces and numbered down the left-hand margin. The members present write in their numbers, but you, not being a member, will simply write Deputy' opposite the nine. The president of the club will be standing beside the table and will hand you a small silver counter stamped with the same number, and having a clip attachment. This you will hang to the edge of your coat— and, by the way, leave it behind you on the table as you quit the room. He will then offer you a velvet bag, from which you'll draw a paper pellet bearing either a number from one to six, or a similar number followed by an R. These indicate the opponents for the night. I think that is all."
"And when is the—er—colleetion taken up ?"
"Collection ? "

"Charity, you know." Calthorpe laughed, but with a little embarrass- ment. "That is not exactly, our method. You must have noticed, Winslow, that there are two things human natur9 loves." ' "Only two!" I interjected. "How modest you are Why, it takes more than that to make a decent salad—or the gout.. Two hundred you mean."

"The bizarre, and an element of chance," went on Calthorpe, as if I had never spoken. "These it is that hold the club together. You play six parties a night, and against as many different opponents, half of you keeping your seats after each game, the other half moving on in rotation. Keep your score in the ordinary way, and at the end a the night the man who has lost most points has to give their value in charity, reckon- ing each point at sixpence and first deducting hit gains from his losses." "But that might mean--" I began. "It's charity," he interrupted, hastily; "and in that the rule of the club is this: The loser must give the whole amount to the first person who applies to him, unless he has previously given it to an object he believes -deserving. There have been some quaint---" "Quaint!" I groaned. "Why, it might mean fifty pounds ! " Again Calthorpe grinned, but this time there was humour in his malice. A man always finds a genial amusement in seeing another man let into a hole.

"I have known it almost a hundred, and as low as seven-and-sixpence. 'That is where the element of chance comes in. You will find it quite interesting, and, by the way, Winslow, of course you understand .this is a private club,. and not to be talked about."

"Private asylum," said I, crossly, and rising to go; "but since it is only for once, and to oblige you, I don't mind." "Oh, you'll like it," he answered; "let the p rit of the thing once grip you and you'll want me to put you up for the first vacancy. Good-bye, then for a—er—day or two. Re- member, play begins at nine, and punctuality is a virtue.

I saw the sense in Calthorpe's last remark, and ten minutes before the time named I entered the club-room. At the door a tall. keen-faced, eiean-snaven man —greeted me with the Kindly welcome of an old friend, shaking my hand warmly.

div.head: Death of an Old Croft Inhabitant.
div.p: Death of an Old Croft Inhabitant.

The remains of the late Mrs. D. Waywell, one of Croft's oldest inhabitants, were interred at ChriAt Church on Monday afternoon. Deceased, who had attained her 71st year, expired as her residence in Heath-lane-about nine p.m. on Friday, after a lingering illness. Having been a resident of the parish for almost fifty years, she was well known and esteemed. Only four weeks have elapsed • since her husband (Mr. D. Waywell) was laid to rest. One son and four daughters are left to mourn their loss.

div.p: 476 ALIENS EXPELLED.

The Home Secretary, in a printed reply to Mr. Thorn- ton, M.P.. says that 287 expulsion orders were made against aliens in the year 1906 ; 93 in the first quarter of the present year. The return for the three monas ending June 30 was 71. In July 25 orders had been Trade bringing the total since the comencement cf the Act up to 476.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
THE WINGS or THE ANT.

In the Comptes Rendus, M. Charles Janet has an interesting note on the muscular ap- paratus of the wings of the queen ant. Al- thc•ugh the wings are only used once in a lifetime of perhaps ten years, this apparatus is the biggest organ in the body. After fer- tilisation the wings are cast aside, and the muscles disappear, being replaced by little (!olumns of adipose tissue. The disappear- ance of the muscles has been attributed to phagocytosis—that is, the absorb* of the tissues by leucocytes. Janet, however, shews that "there is no phagocytosis. but that the material of the muscles goes to enrich the blood.

div.head: FOHN WIND IN KOREA.
div.p: A FOHN WIND IN KOREA.

The Journal of the Meteorologicf.7l Society of Japan contains an account by Dr. Okada of \the occurrenoe in Korea of those remark- able winds which have been called Fan winds. The winds to which this name was originally given are warm winds blowing down from the snow-clad mountains of Swit- zerland, and producing extensive meltings of the snow. They have hence been called "snow-eaters." The Fan is essentially a phenomenon of mountainous regions, and Wonsan; in Korea, where they have been ob- served, is surrounded, except on the east, by high mountains. In this region they are al- ways westerly, and cause abnormally high temperatures and dryness of the air. A similar wind in North America blowing down from the Rocky Mountains has. been called the Chinook. 'Fan winds occur also in the Arctic regions. Blowing sometimes in midwinter they produce a remarkable climatic paradox. As a result of the eleva- tion of temperature caused by them it may happen that Northern Greenland, though in winter- darkness, is warmer than Southern France.

div.head: COLORADO BEETLE,
div.p: THE COLORADO BEETLE,

The Carnegie Institution has published .an account of a series of important investiga- tions on the Colorado beetle and its allies carried out by Dr. W. L. Tower. The _genus to which the much-dreaded potato pest be- longs is known •as Leptinotarsa, and it is thought that Southern Mexico is the centre of the origin of this group of beetles. The food plant. of the Colorado beetle is a species of wild potato, Solanum rostratum. Now the fruit .of this plant ip provided with hooked spines, and it is suggested that it was carried by Spanish caravans and herds of bison to Texas, Arizona, and the Rocky 'Mountains. The beetle

div.head: FOLLOWED ITS FOOD PLANT,
div.p: FOLLOWED ITS FOOD PLANT,

and, extended its geographical range with it. Presently the potato fields of the settlers, and the areas occupied by Solarium rostra- tuai approached each other. The beetle find- ing the cultivated potato much to its taste took to it with avidity. Crops were destroyed, and the pest spread from field to field. In a comparatively short time the Colorado beetle spread over the• whole breadth of the Con- tinent, from the Rockies to the eastern sea- board, from whence it threatened an invasion of Europe. Only the most stringent regula- tions prevented it becoming a plague in the Old World as it had in the New.

div.head: ECONOMY IN LIGHT.
div.p: ECONOMY IN LIGHT.

Mr. MTarlane Moore, an electrician of New Jersey, has for many years \ been ex- perimenting with the view of producing a more perfect light than those now in use. It hss for long been known, says the Globe, that the most economical of these are extra- vagant. That is to say, only a small amount of the energy expended in producing them is really changed into light: In most of them, indeed, only something like 1 per cent. is utilised. Now some interesting investiga- tions which were carried out some years ago at the Alleghany Observatory in America in- dicated that the most economical form of light is that •of the fire-fly and glow-worm. No part of the energy used in producing this light is wasted in the form of heat rays, &c. And the light of the fire-fly is of the nature of a phosphorescent glow. Hence various forms of light founded on this \ principle have been suggested. It has been pointed out that if certain phosphorescent powders are introduced into a Crookes tube, and this is made to glow by passing an electric current through it, such a light will be produced. The electric energy is practically

ALL CHANGED INTO LIGHT. And several years ago Mr. MTarlane Moore devised an electric lamp in which the glass was made to glow—probably by the in- troduction of some phosphorescent powder— instead of the usual ,carbon filament. Ap- parently this lamp was . not a commercial success, but Mr. Moore has been working at the subject since, and has improved his method of lighting. The defect of previous attempts to illuminate by means of glowing vacuum tubes lay in the violent spasmodic flickering always associated with it. This has been Overcome in Mr. Moore's new system by an automatic valve, which admits the exact quantity of air required to prevent the flickering. And by using different kinds of gas for thii purpose differently coloured lights - are produced. Mr. _Moore has ex- plained his methods in a paper read before th.c' American Institution of Electrical Engineers.

div.head: MAKING INCANDESCENT MANTLES.
div.p: MAKING INCANDESCENT MANTLES.

A few years ago the incandeseent Mantle was a chemical speciality, manufactured in small 'quantities, with comparatively small capital, but nevertheless it was a fairly pro- fitable undertaking. The work was mostly done by hand, and no expensive plant was erected. To-day, however, a very large capital is invested in the incandescent mantle industry, says Mr. Harold Baron writing in Cassier's Magazirte. It gives em- ployment to many operatives, and the daily production of mantles is enormous. Describing the process of manufacture, he says the ramie yarn is knitted on special round knitting - machines in the form of an endless stocking. This long stocking is then very carefully washed and cut up into pieces. It now passes into another depart- ment, where it is immersed in the fluid, which gives the mantle its most important property, namely, illuminating power. The chief constituent of this bath is thorium nitrate, a salt which is obtained from mona- zite sand found in Brazil. The •bath also contains small quantities of cerium nitrate and occasionally other

NITRATES OF THE RARE EARTHS. The exact proportions of these constituents is a matter of the greatest importance upon which the success of the mantle depends. The constitntion of this bath is therefore a jealously-guarded secret. The next operation is the-burning off of the mantle, whereby the cotton forming the basis of the mantle 16 consumed, and the salts are converted into oxides. This is carried out on special 'Machines, and the thorium oxide remains in the form of the original texture as a 4ight structure of ash. On a second flame, the so- called press gas flame, ,the mantle is brought into the proper form for use. At this stage tha mantle is in a

div.head: VERY FRAGILE CONDITION,
div.p: VERY FRAGILE CONDITION,

and cannot be handled, much less tran- sported, without damage. The mantle is, ' therefore, immersed in collodion, or some such fluid as leavei, the thoria covered with a film of readily combustible Inaterial. In this form,. and carefully packet, the mantles , are exported to America, Australia, and all parts of the globe. A very large variety of mantles are now upon the market, and most of these are of uniformly good qualitY. Mantles for burners of the " inverted ' type are now being extensively introduced. The light riven by an inverted burner with a good mantle is the most economical source or lignt known at the present day. The light is ex- ceedingly steady, and in -general appearance resembles the Nernst electric lamp.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
AUGUET 10th. 1907

An indication of the strong GREAT BRITAIN feeling which exists in many AND RUSSIA. quarters in regard to any possible alliance between this country and Russia was to be discerned in a question asked in the House of Commons on Wednesday by Mr. T. F. RICHARDS, one of the members of the Independent Labour party. Mr. RICHARDS asked the Foreign Secretary whether he could see his way clear to inform the Ru,ssian authorities that unless better treatment is meted out to the Russian people this country may deem it necessary to refuse to form any alliance with Russia whatsoever. Sir EDWARD GREY replied through Mr. RUNCIMAN that the interna affairs of Russia have nothing to do with negotia_ tions between the two Governments, and added the important and satisfactory declaration that "the question of an alliance has not been raised." This puts an end to many recent rumours of a rather definite character and Mr. RICHARDS may be congratulated on having drawn it forth, though it has always been obvious, of course, that an alliance with Russia of the character implied— of such a character, that is to say, as the alliance between Russia and France—was a political Mr. RICHARDS, as it seems, would throw Russia over altegether, submitting it to a diplomatic boycott, Ostracising it from the family of nations so far as we are concerned. But that is another political impossibility. There are matters that must be discussed and arranged, not necessarily dealing with treaties and alliances, and these cannot in our own interests be neglected, nor can we claim a right to dictate to Russia as to its manner of dealing with its own people. Such a course could only lead to such a snub as would be a national humiliation. On the other hand, there is a great deal to be said for , the view that any special arrangement made with the Russian Government at the present time would operate disastrously to the popular interests in the agonising struggle between the Russian people and the bureaucracy. It would tend to restore Russian credit and to place the Government in further command of the sinews of war < It would no less tend to discourage the people of Russia in their struggle towards freedom atd constitutionalism. The reasonableness of this point of view has already been recognised by our own Government, as when it countermanded the arrangements for the visit of a British Fleet to Russian waters.

His MAJESTY'S MINISTERS have, and must have for a long time to come, a difficult course to steer in regard to our Russian relationship. We have never been among those who expected the Russian revolutionaries to make such quick work as was made in the French Revllution. The conditions are almost as widely different as they could possibly be. There has already been, it is prob- able, a much huger sacrifice of life since " Red Sunday " than took place in France between the march of the Reds of the Midi, and the Napoleonic " whiff of grapeshot," and many of the incidents have been much more horrible than those of even the worst days of the Reign of Terror. Yet what advance has been made towards the liberation of the Russian people ? The country is a chaos bestrewn with blood, yet the bureaucracy has not been visibly weakened. Even the CZAR has not been terrorised, as appears from recent accounts of his demeanour during his cruise. His father became a gloomy madman in times that were safe and peacefulin comparison to these but the 1111'EROR Nrcuouls is, it seems, in the most cheerful of spirits, as was Nero during the burning of Rome. Russia has still a long agony before her not to be terminated, it is probable, until some leader arises who is powerful enough to draw the people away from the priests and into a common association for the defence of life and the establishment of public rights. Probably he will come from the army, when he does come, but as yet he gives no sign. Our own duty, whilst things remain as they are, clearly is to do nothing which would have a tendency to make them worse.
It was with a sense of shock THE LATE COLONEL that Warringtonians heard RIDGWAY. of the painfully sudden

death of Colonel J. C. Ridgway, the late respected commander of the local Volunteers. He had long been a familiar figure in the town and all who had the privilege of his friendship entertained the highest respect for him. Be was a sturdy, outspoken, and kindly English gentleman and during the time he con- trolled the Volunteer Battalion he threw himself whole-heartedly into its work. His own untiring service was an inspiration to the men to do their utmost for the honour of the battalion, and he was justly proud of the splendid response of the Volunteers to the call to active service during the South African campaign. The ;Colonel led a busy life to the last, for in addition to being the head of a leading commercial concern he discharged numerous public duties. Warring- ton mourns the loss of one of its worthiest towns- men and heartfelt indeed will be the sympathy with the widow and family in their great and unexpected bereavement.
It has taken some time to THE LATE CHIEF settle certain affairs conse- CONSTABLE. quent on the death of the

fate Chief Constable, Mr. Luke Talbot, at Cairo, and chief among these has been the provision for his widow. Mrs. Talbot was entitled to certain sums in lieu of the pension to which the lute officer would have been entitled, and we are glad to see that she will receive, in all, a lump sum of £515, comprised of grants for £53 from the Corporation of Bradford, £4O from the Corporation of Kendal, and £425 from the Corporation of Warrington. With regard to the latter sum we were somewhat startled on reading the minutes of the Watch Committee which are to be presented at Tuesday's Council meeting. A resolution of the 18th July specifies the granting of an annuity to Mrs. Talbot of the sum of £425. This struck us as being so uncommonly generous on the part of the Corpora- tion and so fortunate for the lady in question that we made inquiries at the Town Hall only to learn that the words an annuity were printed in error and should have been a gratuity. There is a great and obvious difference between the two, and the indignation of the economists can be readily imagined if they were asked to sanction a life pay- ment of so large a sum even to the widow of such a respected officer as the late Chief Constable.
Foresight has never, unfor- LAYING OUT tunately,been a conspicuous SUBURBS. characteristic of the builders

of English towns and suburbs. Most urban districts present a painful spectacle of houses built at inconvenient angles, sometimes picturesque' but more often unsightly, and obstructive to traffic. What sums have been spent on removing obstructions of this kind since the era of trams and public conveyances of the more popular sort began it is almost impossible to estimate, but the T.)wn Clerk of Leeds hazarded the guess a day or two since ' that they could not have amounted to less ' than £30,000,000. The fear now is that, unless powers are given to the local authorities to regu- late the building of streets in the suburbs, we shall, with all the lessons of the past before us, repeat the errors which have proved so costly. The deputation which waited upon the Premier , and Mr. Burns got a sympathetic reply, and a promise of legislation which, if the exigencies of the next session will permit, *will doubtless be redeemed. We do not want our streets laid out Iwith the monotonous regularity of American cities; nor, perhaps, do we crave for an abso- lute copy of those hard-and-fast rules which are made by German municipal authorities in regard to the suburbs of Teutonic towns. But we do want something that will save future local administrators from the painful experiences of the past. With the increase of motor traffic, the suburbs are becoming of greater importance in the eyes of those who are responsible for traffic, and it is abundantly clear that the demands which will be made upon road space in the future will be considerably larger than at any time in the past. Therefore we ought no to permit the arteries through which the traffic passes from the town to the country to be crowded and cramped by build- ings erected in unsuitable situations. The munici- palities, in asking for powers to protect posterity in this:matter,are making no unreasonable demand.
The decision of the House THE SEAMENS' of Lords in the recent CHARTER. contraband of war case will

be applauded by all lovers of justice. The circuraltances of the action were peculiar. During the progress of the Russo- Japanese campaign the steamship Franklyn took on board a cargo of coal at Cardiff for Hong Kong. Her crew had signed articles for three years for a voyage to any ports or places within certain degrees of latitude, including Hong Kong, and to end at such port in the United Kingdom or the Continent of Europe as might be required by the master. Coal was, of course, contraband of war, and vessels carrying coal to ports under the control of either combatant in the Far East were being seized by the belligerents. When the Franklyn arrived at Hong Kong it was made known that her cargo was destined for Sasebo, a Japanese and thither the crew were ordered to take her. They refused in a body, and were promptly thrown into gaol for seventy days for having impeded the progress of the voyage. They were, -in their release, sent to England as distressed seamen. The Franklyn returned to England a year later, and the crew then brought an action against the company to recover wages from the time they were left at Hong Kong, and for damages. They won their case in the High Court; but only with wages down to their arrival in this country. The case was carried to the Appeal Court by the defendants, and the crew entered a counter:- appeal for wages for a longer period. They won again, and were accorded wages down to the date cf the Appeal Court judgment, and "maintenance." The House of Lords has upheld , that decision, and the Lord Chancellor regretted that they could not give damages to their men for their sufferings in Hong Kong, Had that been possible, he intimated that they would have been exemplary. The judgment is a charter for the mercantile sailor of the future. Too often he has been victimised, and the decision of the Lords, beyond which it is impossible to go, will show owners that they cannot treat the men who engage for their ships without the common justice which Englishmen have a right to demand. The present instance was made worse by the imprisonment at Hong Kong and the fact that the men were stranded on their release from gaol. The lesson for shipowners is salutary, and the general public will regret with the Lord Chancellor that the law did not permit of the men being awarded sub- stantial damages in addition to their wages.

div.head: Bank Holiday.
div.p: Bank Holiday.

The August Bank holiday always witnesses a great exodus to the seaside and other popular resorts, but Monday appears to have created a record. Fortun- ately, the weather was propitious and it was, there- fore, not to be wondered at that thousands of War- ringtonians availed themselves of the opportunity of spending a day amid more congenial surroundings. Many people went away for the week-end, but the heaviest holiday traffic was dealt with on Monday. The rallway companies catered for all tastes by the variety of cheap excursions. The following are the principal bookings :—London and North-Western: Blackpool, 600; Frodsham, 500 • Llangollen, 100; Morecombe and Windermere, 260 and the Royal Lancashire show at Bolton, 200; there were also heavy bookings to Scotland. Cheshire Lines : Liver- pool, 2,000; New Brighton, 1,200; Southport, 1,000; Douglas, 900 and Manchester 1,100. The morning opened promisingly and although later on there were threatening clouds, the sun triumphed and the holiday makers were enabled to enjoy themselves to the full under delightful conditions. For those who preferred to stay in Warrington the Football Club sports were a great attraction. In the evening there were large audiences at the re-opening of the Royal Court Theatre and also at Mr. Joshua Dyson's entertainments in the Parr Hall.

How much longer are the. condemned shops at the top of Bridge-street going to cumber the ground and spoil the chief thoroughfare of the town. Coming up Horsemarket-street, the stranger might for a moment imagine that he was approaching some historic. ruin for the gable end of Mr. Lee's shop has a singularly battered and battlemented look. The remains of old placards and plasters soon destroy the illusion, how- evea. From the Rylands-street side, the view is nothing but an eyesore. We suppose the new shops must be up, before the old ones come down. Patience ! Patience ! and impatience ! !

The purchase of the 'Mes-srs. Edelsten's Pin Mill and the Mersey Bedstead Works has now been com- pleted, and these familiar landmarks in Knutsford-road may shortly be expected to disappear. The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee has resolved to demolish the Pin Mill and sell the slrplus land for shops and buildings, while so much of the Bedstead Works as encroaches upon the building line is also to be removed forthwith. This latter is a most urgent improvement, for no more dangerous thoroughfare exists in Warrington than the narrow section fronting the Bedstead Works and adjoining shops. There are two unusual items on the Council agenda for next week. Among a number of increases of salary is a recommendation Trom Mr. F. Taylor, the secretary of the Gas Works, that £5O be deducted from his salary and added to that of Mr. W.S. Howard, at the same time appointing the latter assistant secretary. Occasions are rare on which public officials suggest a reduction of salary, and Mr. Taylor is entitled to warm praise for his economical suggestion. The second item which is out of the ordinary relates to the application by the Electricity Committee for authority to borrow £4,889 for extensions at Howley. It has been found that the tenders are considerably below the estimate, and conssquently only £3070 10s., will be required on loan. This is another satisfactory saving.

Our citizen soldiers have this week been encamped at Llanberis. There were not many pangs of regret when it became known that Salisbury Plain would not be visited on this occasion; on the contrary the Volunteers wera delighted with the prospect of a holiday at such a delightful place as Llanberis. The weather has been far from ideal and the natural beauties with which the district is so richly endowed have not been seen to the best advantage—at any rate, during the latter part of the week. The men have, however, put in plenty of hard work and have engaged in some highly interesting manoeuvres. How well they have played their part in the brigade operations may be gathered from the fact that General Burnett, who directed the plan of campaign, did not hesitate to express the opinion that they were ready for active service. * *

The queption of vaccination fees has long exercised the minds of the members of the Warrington Board of Guardians. There is a general opinion that the amount expended under this head is excessive, and the Board set to work to effect an economy. A special committee was appointed and on its recommendation the Guardians unanimously decided on Wednesday to reduce the fee for each successful vaccination to 3s within the borough and 3s. 6d. in the rural districts. instead of the present rate of ss. The doctors, naturally resent the change, but it is the duty • of the Guardians to consider the interests of the ratepayers, and vaccination has been such a heavy charge that we believe their action will be generalty approved. From the remarks made at Wednesday's meeting it appears not unlikely that the whole question will be reconsidered at some future time, with a view to instituting a new system of appointment.

Councillor W. J. Wilson seems to have specialised on the great workmen's tram-ticket question. His latest suggestion is that the holders of workmen's tickets be allowed to use the return half on any journey in or out at any time. It seems to us that the workmen get the greatest benefit out of the cars already, and we should hardly imagine they are in the majority as passengers. If the Committee would run special workmen's cars at certain times of the day they would be conferring a real benefit. The work- man in his oily over-ails and smelly corduroys ought to sit with others similarly attired and not with the clean and tidy general public. The poor penny-paying passenger has often enough little chance of even getting on board a car in wet weather during the workman's meal hour, and if he does secure a seat he is probably sorry he did not walk by the time the terminus is reached.

e How are the children's teeth ? is an important question nowadays. The Cambridge Children's Dental Institute the other day began its work of examining the teeth of Cambridge school children, and some startling results were declared. Of the first thirteen children examined, none over eight years of age, only two had entirely sound teeth. In every other case the permanent molars of each child were diseased. In all except one case these teeth were capable of being saved if attended to, but in a year or two most of them would be hopelessly decayed. The parents are said to be co-operating cordially with the Institute, and every effort is being made to conciliate the youngsters themselves. * * *
We have heard that : There was once a cabman who was satisfied with his fare.
There was once a barber who didn't remark on the weather.
There was once an actress who was not photo- graphed showing her teeth. There was once a politician who kept his election promises.
- There was once a doctor who failed to send in his bill.

There was once a journalist who never used mole words than was absolutely necessary. There was once an actor who acted for art's sake. There was once an amateur cricketer who did not get paid for "clerical duties." There was once a professor who was not infallible. There was once a man who owned a motor-car who had never exceeded the speed limit. _ _
