of Warrington, who has recently lie-en employed by Mr. Benjamin Barker, Haydock-street, Earlestotvn, was charged before Mr. John White with stealing a blanket valued at 105.16 d. the property of her employer. —Prisoner when asked to plead said she did not intend to steal the blanket but she meant taking it back again when she got her wages.—Mary Barker said she lived at Earlestown with her father to whom the blanket belonged. She last saw it in the bath- room on Tuesday. At eleven o'clock the same day she missed it and prisoner had also disappeared.--P.O. Lennie said he received information from Miss Barker and afterwards arrested prisoner who had two bundles in her possession, one containing the blanket and the other her own clothing.—Prisoner was remanded to the Warrington County Petty Sessions. GARDEN TENTS.—Tennis, Croquet, and other out- door sports.—.l. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Dyson's Dioramas and Gipsy Choir. Warrington people have this week been afforded the opportunity of renewing their acquaintance with Mr. Joshua Dyson's Dioramas and Gipsy Choir, and large audiences have attended the entertainments given nightly in the Parr Hall. Mr. Dyson and his talented company have visited our town on many occasions and here, as throughout the kingdom, have i achieved a splendid reputation for the excellence of the programmes submitted for the enjoyment of their patrons. The success of Mr. Dyson's enterprise, wonderful as it has been, is highly gratify- ing, for refinement is the keynote of the enter- tainments, and it is therefore evident that the public appreciate the work of one who for many years has I made it his aim to provide attractions of the highest' class. All who have witnessed this week's perform- I ances agree that the standard established on previous visits has been fully maintained. Instruction and amusement are pleasingly combined, for by means of the Dioramas the audiences are transported in imagination to new and delightful scenes, and Mr. Dyson's concise descriptions of the places of interest are flavoured with humour- ous touches and are interstersed with musical items by the choir. Every evening there is a fresh I series of pictures, catering for a variety of tastes. I Unstinted praise can be bestowed on the efforts of the choir who preface the lantern entertainment with a choice miscellaneous programme. There are scings, —national, sentimental and humorous—choruses, and instrumental selections,—all affording evidence of the all-round abilities of the company. The entertain- ments throughout go with a merry swing, and the closing sketch never fails to create the greatest merri- ment. Mention should be made of the admirable series of new animated pictures given each evening, which have proved very popular. Another novel and original feature is provided by Mysterious Parker, who is a remarkably clever quick-change artiste. All who have not visited the Parr Hall this week should make a point of doing so before Mr. Dyson's company leaves. There will be a special performance for chil- dren this afternoon, and in the evening the concluding diorama entertainment will be given, Old England" being the subject. On Sunday the choir will bring its visit to a close with sacred concerts in the after- noon and evening.

div.head: INCREASE OF RECHABITISM.
div.p: THE INCREASE OF RECHABITISM.
Notable Figures for the Biennal Conference.

The proceedings commenced at Newcastle-on-Tyne on Monday in connecnion with the forty-second High Movable Conference of the Independent Order of Reohabites, and the board of directors are able to present a report marking a progress during the last two years which transcends all previous work of the Order. A larger number of tents has been instituted in the last two years than in any similar period since the registra- tion of the Order, and the increase in membership also beats the record of any previous time, the total increase being 46,841, of whom 19,324 are adults and 27,517 juveniles. The total membership is now 393,054, there being 183,809 adults in Great Britain and 40,399 abroad with' 150,619 juveniles in Great Britain and 18,227 abroad. The district forming the greatest number of tents—both juvenile and adult—in the period is the Durham County district. With regard to tempemnee legislation, the hope is expressed that the promised Government Bill will be a comprehensive measure,and the Order's previous resolu- tions in favour of direct veto and Sunday closing are affirmed. With regard to juvenile work, it is reported that provincial conferencez.have proved very successful, and t is further stated that there is a growing interest in juvenile competitions. MR. BOTTOMLEY'S CRITICISM OF THE LABOUR MEETING. Mr.J.H. Bottomley,speaking in reference to the Labour demonstration at Haydock Park, said the demonstration was largely composed of pit lads. There was a great deal of smoke, there were large clouds of inflammable gas, here and there a slight electrical flash. There were volumes of scalding water, mud and ashes thrown about in all directions, and here and there among the ashes and mud of extravagance and nonsense a piece of pure gold, ready melted. But he did not complain. The speaker did not place him on a keg of gunpowder and blow him up, nor did they purpose to hire him out as a target for the Army. Yet he would willingly attend their political funeral, not as a mouruer, but as under- taker. (Laughter.) Scratch any of the three M.P.'s present and they would find a Socialist, but not a word was said of jubilation over the recent openly-avowed Socialist victory in Colne Valley respecting trades- unionist principles. He was at one with them. He believed in a high level of industrial efficiency, and he agreed that the organization of workers was a matter of imperative necessity, but trades unions should not be party political organizations. There was a great deal of talk about old age pensions and lack of funds to provide them. These Socialists talked about Germany, yet the German workers paid no more for their bread, their coffee, their sugar, their clothing, and their boots than we did in England. Yet from their tariffs imposed on foreign imports they gained old-age pensions and all the inestimable advantage of insurance against sickness and accident. (Applause). Those so-called Labour members who lived on money contributed by trades unionists of all parties preached doctrines repugnant to a great section of their pay-masters, who would at an election, under secrecy of ballot, vote all right. (Hear, hear). Every speaker at Haydock betrayed his anxiety about the Newton Division. The verdict of the men who attended was that the refreshments were better than the speeches. (Laughter and applause)

div.head: Church Army Mission.
div.p: Church Army Mission.

The Church Army Mission of St. Peter's had on' Monday a fully enjoyed holiday under the leadership of Captain Higson. A three-horsed brake attended for the party at the Mission ^room in John-street at 8 a.m. and proceeded to Little 'Hutton via Worsley, arriving at the Parish room about 12.30. A. number of cyclists accompanied. , At Worsley a halt was made to view the Ellesmere Memorial and the Church. After luncheon, Peel Hall, the residence of Mr. S. Armitage, was by his kind permission visited and a rose freshly cut was given by Miss Armitage to each, and some suitable hymns were sung. After inspect- ing the conservatories &c., hearty thanks were given to the olyner and Miss Armitage and best wishes ' expressed for, the better health of Mrs Armitage. The ancient and picturesque seat of Lord Kenyon was next inspected, to view which kind permission had been accorded. Returning to the Parish Room tea was partaken of and then the party attended at the Church where a simple service was feelingly conducted by the Vicar, Rev. S. P. Wilson, who delivered an instructive address. The famous Charlton Memorial Window and the Reredos were explained by the Vicar. An open- air meeting conducted by Captain Voig, C.A., was held in the street adjoining the Parish Room and many of 1 the inhabitants were present. Captains Olive (Eccles), Edmondson (Bolton) and Matcham (Peel) were amongst the party

We would remind or readers that on Thursday 'next the annual show promoted by the Warrington and District Agricultural Society will be held in Walton Park. Prizes' cups, &c., to the value of £750 are offered. There are classes• for shires, hunters, hackneys, harness horses, jumpers, trades- men's and tenant famers' turnouts, cattle, pigs, cheese .and butter. The Yorkshire Hussars Band will be in attendance. The Walton Flower Show will also be held in Walton Park on Thursday. Shrewsbury's great floral fete will be held on Wednesday and Thursday, August 21st and 22nd. The flower show is the .grandest in Europe, over £1,200 being offered in prizes. Several famous bands Will, be in attendance and there will also be a series of sensational porformances by leading artistes. Special excursion trains wiliabe run from Warrington .and all parts. There will be a revival of "Ye Olde Rushbearing Pestival "on the May Queen Ground at Lymm to-day. It is nearly 20 years since this old-time custom last took plebe, and interesting scenes are promised. The Procession starts from the Lymm Cross. TOASTING CHEESE, 4d.,5d.,6d. per lb. ASHLEY'S.—Advt. _ Our ieaders will regret to learn that 3fr. James Dodds has since Monday been suffering from a severe attack of jaundice. Yesterday, his condition was reported to be improved. On inquiry last night we learned that there was /la improvement in the condition of tho Rev. E. J. Willeocks, headmaster of the Grammar School. New Co-operative Manager. • Out of a large number of applicants Mr. W. Atkinson, for five years manager to the Birkenhead Co-operative Society, has been appointed manager to the Warrington Co-operative Society.
Liberals, Register! All Liberals entitled to vote are urged to examine the lists just published and if their names do not appear they should communicate with Mr. J. Howes, 3un., Liberal Club.

Matriculation Results. Through a clerical error in the office of the Joint Matriculation Board, the name of Miss Hilda Mary 'Stansfield, daughter of Mr/ W. H. Stansfield, was Omitted from the list of successes of the Universities of Manchester, Liverpool, Leeds and Sheffield. Our readers will be pleased to hear that Miss Stansfield passed in the First Division.

'The Canal Burst in Cheshire. The restoration of the burst in the bank of the Staffordshire Canal at llarbury, near Northwich, is almost complete. Water was on Thursday turned in to test the sides of the canal. Some thousands of tons of material have been employed in the repairing, which has taken 18 days. ,A great dislocation of traffic has resulted from the burst, the Staffordshire pottery trade being chiefly affected. BOILING BACON, 10., 5d., 6d.per lb. ASIII:BY'S.—Advt.

Footrace. On Saturday afternoon, on the Warrington Football Field, a quarter-mile match for £4O was decided between Elliott Harris, a Warrington footballer, and T. Williams, a local athlete. Williams led for a hundred yards, but Harris scion made up the leeway, and shot past his rival, who stumbled and fell. The footballer finished an easy winner by about twenty yards.

Accident to a Cyclist. Richard Dunn, a clerk in the employ of the St. lielens Cable Works and residing at 87:Mersey-street, was riding his bicycle along Slutcher's-lane, when he collided with a horse and cart, and received injuries to his face and fractured his thigh. First aid was rendered by the police and he was admitted to the Infirmary where he is detained.

Assault on a Military Policeman. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, before the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) and other magistrates —Richard Roberts, 29, Eldon-street, and George Ellis, 24, Elizabeth-street, were summoned for assaulting a military policeman, named Patrick Hines, on Saturday night. It appears that Hines was patrolling Buttermarket-street oaSaturday night when. -the defendants asked him if he had " gripped " any- one. He asked what it had got to do with them,when they became abusive, knocked him down, and kicke3 him. Roberts was fined 10s. and costs, and Ellis se. and costs.
FARM-FED FAT BAcoN,sd.per lb. at ASIILEY'S.—Advt. Poor Children's Camp.

On Saturday morning the first contingent of boys assembled at the Drill Hall in charge of Mr. A. H. Lee together with his assistants, Messrs. W. Turner, W. J. Turner, Houghton, Jolley, Newton, Griffiths and Mee. The roll having been called, the children proceeded to Bank Quay Station and journeyed to Prestatyn by the 10.28 train. After an enjoyable holiday they returned home last evening, arriving in Warrington at eight o'clock. The next contingent i;vill leave Warrington to-day by the 10.28 train as before. It is only hope that the clerk of the weather will look upon Prestatyn more kindly than of late. If so, the children will enjoy themselves to the full. Services for Sunday.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
ST. HELENS.

ST. HELENS INN STRUCK BY LIGHTNING. Shortly before ten o'clock on Tuesday a thunderstorm accompanied by heavy showers of rain, broke over St. Helens. During the storm the White Lion Inn, Fleet- lane, was struck by lighting and considerably damaged. The occupants were greatly alarmed, but fortunately escaped without injuries. DEATH OF A ST. HELENS GUARDIAN. Mr. Richard-Hamblett Houghton, who for the pt six years had represented the Hardshaw Ward of St. Helens borough on the Prescot Board of Guardians, died on Nionday after suffering since April last from dropsy and heart disease. Mr. Houghton carried on business as a boot and shoe maker at 28, Westfield-street and was a member of one of the most prominent local Wesleyan families. He was fifty-three years of age, and leaves a widow mul two sons. HIS BROTHER-IN-LAW'S e*HOST.

James Logan, a St. Helens labourer, was on Monaay morning sent by the magistrates to the workhouse for fourteen days, he having been found in Canal-street at three o'clock that morning wandering about and, in fear of the ghost of his brother-in-law' who had been dead a number of years. Logan had been drinking hard.—Ellen Wilkinson, a. Bolton woman, was also dealt with in a similar manner. HIGHER ELEMENTARY SCHOOL FGR ST. HELENS..

The St. Helens Education Authority have been pressed for a considerable time by the Board of Educa% lion to provide a higher elementary school for the borough. A site has heen in hand for some time, but the committed have decided to open next month a higher elementary school at the Gamble Institute and have undertaken to begin the erection of school build- ings within a specified time. Mr. R. W. Ferguson has been appointed head master of the school, and a full staff is now being appointed., WOMAN SENT TO GAOL.

Mary M`Cabe, an elderly widow, of Blackbrook-road, was a St. Helens on Monday sent to gaol for three months' hard labour for stealing groceries from a store in King-street. On Saturday night a woman named Leyland saw the woman go into the store and take 2s. Bd. worth of groceries. She was arrested with the articles in her possession, and as she had a record of twenty-eight convictions at Liverpool and other places, she was dealt with severely. SCAMP SENTENCED.

John Dearden, a young man, of 119, Central-street, strenuously denied a charge of indecency preferred against him at St. Helens, on Monday. Dearden was alleged to have committed the offence in College-street on Friday night, but he deuied that he was out of the house at the time, and called his mother to bear out this statement, but she broke down under cross. examination. Dearden had been convicted four times, and was sent to gaol for three months hard labour. SOLD THE HEN AND CHICKENS.

James Kinder, collier, of 47, Langtree street, was charged at St Helens on Monday with deserting his. wife and children. Mrs. Kinder said they had been married eight years. Her husband was always threaten- ing to kill her. On Wednesday he turned her out, and later he sold a hen and chickens for six shillings sad drank the money. He afterwards tried to sell the pictures in order to get more drink. She had sent the children for mooey, but he had refused it.—Kinder alleged that this was the third time his wife had felt him, and that she would not help to keep the home straight. The case was adjourned for a fornight.

div.head: BANK HOLIDAY.
div.p: BANK HOLIDAY.

St. Helens people on Monday exhibited the usual anxiety to get away from the smoke to enjoy a pleasant day by the seaside or in some more ttractive place than glassopolis. The bookings at the ..railway station for Blackpool, Southport, and the Lake District were very heavy, while a large number went to North Wales, where the members of the two Volunteer Battalions had proceeded the day before. The electric tramcars to Liverpool were largely patronised by people anxious to see the decorations of the city and to attend the Pagent performances. PRESCOT FLOWER SHOW..

The Twenty-third annual flower show of the Prescot Horticultural Society was held on Monday amid charm- ing surroundings, in Knowsley Park, and under the personal patronage of the Earl of Derby and the Hon. Arthur Stanley, M.P. In addition to the flower show sports and others attractive items were carried out, but the attendance, doubtless owing to other attractions at Liverpool and elsewhere, fell considerably below the average. The horticultural exhibits formed a most beautiful collection, and the standard of quality was exceptionally high, but the numbers showed a considerable falling off. Last year 880 entries were staged, but the backward season spoiled the vegetables and cut flower sections, and reduced the number of entries of 540. Prescot, however, is always famous for its roses, and an infinity of care and skill had been expended on the roses and carnations, the display of these choice blooms being almost up to the usual high standard. The residents of Huyton, Roby, and Rainhill always support the show right royally, and in the green- house plants and grape sections carried off most of the prizes. Mr. J. Butterwood Pratt is again the president of the society, and Mr. William Case a most efficient

secreLary. The judges were Messrs. E. F. Hazleton (Knowsley Hall), J. Bracegirdle (Elm Hall, Wavertree), Joseph Stoney (Camp Hill, Woolton), H. R. Lover (Windlehnrst, St. Helens), D. Little (Ecoleston and T. Holland (Sherdley) ; while Mr. W. and T. Holland (Sherdley) ; while Mr. W. Tyrer, adjudiv. oated on the honey.

ROSA CANINA. NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
"A Socialist Trades Unionist "writes to say that he will reply to " Labourer " and " Politician " next week.

It was a summer evening when Jack Marston and I stood upon the little railway which winds dizzily along the cliff to the quarries of Craig- malin. They are now turning out some of the best granite in Britain, though several experts had declared the natural difficulties in the way of bringing it to the sea to be insuperable. Jack, however, delighted in difficulties, and as he had won his reputation in the construction of a mountain railway funds were forthcoming when he laid before the Highland landowner a scheme which he simply stated was feasible. I drew back instinctively a trifle from the edge, and Jack smiled at me, though the stones his foot dislodged fell past the wheeling birds into the green water very far below. "It looked a good deal worse when we first tackled it," he said, quietly.

One could understand it. That desolation of frowning precipices would, I fancied, have daunted most other men, but Jack had surveyed it undismayed with his steady grey eyes, and a legion of workmen had done his bilding. So in the teeth of blinding deluge and howling gale he had reft a way for the metals along the mountain- side, and Major Northcote, who was largely interested in the venture, would have given him anything he asked for, even to the hand of his daughter. Jack, however, did 4ot ask for it. As a rule he asked for nothing, but took his own, hnd did not shine in feminine society. I had seen him looking strangely out of place in London drawing-rooms, but now as he stood, lean and bronzed and masterful, in soil-stained overalls on the steel road he had built, he looked a man whom anyone could place implicit con- fidence in.
"I suppose they will give me my letters at the post-office, if I ask for them ? " I said, having only arrived the previous night.

'(Of course!" iaid Jack. -'lsn't that the usual object of a post-office'?" "I don't know," said I. "At the last one I went to I found a very naïve damsel in em- barrassingly simple costume engaged in cleaning fish. She ordered me to wait until she had finished and washed her hands, which was apparently necessary, and then stated that the people thereabouts were too well brought up to post letters on a Monday." Jack laughed. "You will find our postmistress somewhat different," said ,he. "You may as well wait down there until Northcote's launch comes for us."

The ferry-house and post-office of Craigmalin as a low, rambling building of the massive masonry which alone seems capable of withstand- ing the Highland climate, and the place had a well-cared-for look about it. Warm sunlight shone down upon the tide which went lapping past it, and the great black hills above rose bare of the usual whirling mist, sharply cut against the blue to their highest summits. An elderly man of frail appearance was digging in the garden and directed me to the house. His gatments were threadbare, but something suggested that he had seen better days. The stone passage I entered was shadowy, but the sunlight shone dazzlingly into the room it led to, and I stood still a moment looking at the girl who rose when she saw me. She wore a plain white dress, but it clung lovingly to her lissom figure, and—for the sunlight was on it—she had splendid red-gold hair. That was all I saw, but it decided me that she was a summer visitor.

"I must apologise for intruding, but can you tell me where the postmistress is ? " I said. The girl smiled, and I saw that her eyes were as fine as her hair ;.so fine, in fact, that one did not notice their colour. Though there was amusement in them, her face was a trifle sad. "I am the postmistress," she said, quietly, in the tone of a well-taught woman, and perhaps noticed my astonishment, for she smiled again. "Then might I trouble you for any letters directed to H. Crossthwaite ? " I said.

The girl handed me several, and I noticed that her wrists were red and her fingers had evidently been engaged pretty constantly in something useful. There was a fine view from a window, and it may have been this which made me desirous to stay there a little, while the girl's next speech afforded an opportunity. "If you are likely to require any provisions we supply the herring boats and coasters," she said; and, seeing that the place was also a general store, I guessed l had been taken for a yachts- man—which, in fact, I was.

"I would like a few pounds of biscuits, the best you have, and some coffee. Two or three pounds of sugar too," I said. It seemed surprising that the girl should take it seriously, but she did, and we opened a good many biscuit tins together before I took up as large a parcel as I could conveniently carry. Then I went out reluctantly to wait for Jack and North- cote's launch, wondering what to do with the goods. The motor-launch came panting up to the ferry beach presently, while when I had greeted Major Northcote and his daughter, and had been presented to Captain Carleton, Jack, who was now attired conventionally, glanced at the bulky parcel. "Whatever have you got there P" he said. • "Biscuits and coffee," I said, somewhat awkwardly, and Miss Northcote laughed a little, while the Major's eyes twinkled, and Jack stared at me.
"Are you afraid of me starving you? There is appatiently a stone of biscuits in that thing," he said.
"I am rather fond of them, and the post- mistress seemed to expect me to buy something, so I did," I said.
"I don't think most men would blame you," said Carleton, and Miss Northcote smiled again. She was passably 'ratty, and supposed to be intellectual.
"You are all the game. I don't think I have heard your opinion of Miss Allister, Mr. Marston," she said.

Now Jack, though a clever engineer, was simple in some respects, and a slight flush crept into his bronzed face. "I think there is some- thing distinctly wrong when a lady of Miss Allister's description is forced to sell biscuits to any lounger who likes to buy them," he said. Miss Northeote, I fancied, was not pleased. "There often is, usually in the antecedents of the lady's friends," she said. Jack, who made no answer, leant over the little oil engine, which it seemed to me was panting in'a distressful fashion.
"I hofie that beastly thing is not going to choke again," said Carleton.
I neticed that his . eyes, which had worn a chronically tired expression, were now scmewhat anxious as be glanced in Miss Northcote's direction. "The tides run strong through here ? " I said.
"They do," said Carleton. "This place looks bmo,eent at slack water. but the flood strelm

goes tnroagn at aix nmes an hour, and the commotion it kicks up would scare any ordinary man. Current shoots up from rocks at the bottom, and makes whirlpools that look capable of sucking a boat down. I don't, however, know if they would, because I haven't tried them."

The engine was grunting hoarsely, and I was not quite easy as I looked about me. A mountain fell she(r to the water on the shore behind us, and on the other a frowning wall of rock rose above the Sound. Between them the green current was already surging at a tolerable pace. Tiere it swung round in eddies, there it boiled, and in one place a white seething suggested a slightly covered reef. When Jack stopped the engine the launch swung round and round, and Major Northcote did not seem happy, though his daughter smiled. "You need not worry, father. Mr. Marston is a match for the most obstinate machine," she

It struck me that here was an opportunity for ;Jack to Say something appropriate, but he did not take it, and I fancied that Miss Northcote was slightly annoyed. He crouched beside the cngine, which spat drops of grimy oil all over krill), while I wondered if Miss Northcote guessed what he was saying. Presently, while the re- -itarted engine sputtered, he stood up Nv ith a black smear on his face and looked at the Major. "I feel I ought to warn you, sir, that this badly- designed affair will drown somebody if they ever vive it an opportunity," he said. "I bought it because the makers declared it did not get out of order, or need a trained engineer," said the Major. It neees tour or the, and a foundry," said r.:arleton.

There was, however, no further stoppage, and the cratt sped mem iy through the whirling, rippling water until we slid into a basin behind a reef. High up on the hillside above it stood. the villa Northcote inhabited. He gave us a good dinner,and when we sat out on the terrace after- wards listening to the deep murmur of Craig- malin Sound his daughter sa,cl to me:

"I like to hear the roar of the stream. It suggests strength and stress and haste, and one finds .it refreshing after drifting through a London season amidst people who consider it bad taste to be in earnest about anything." Perhaps without meaning it she glanced in Jack's direction, and he was speaking to the Major in his usual incisive tones. Then she smiled as her eyes rested upon Carleton, who lay apparently half asleep upon the turf, and I fancied I could guess her thoughts. Presently I induced Northeote to talk of the post-mistress. "She was brought up here, and her father was skipper of a steam coaster," he said. "The oiithe:e of the gentleman who owns the quarries fancy to the girl and had her educated in .cAunburgh. I believe a good deal was expected from her, for she was clever, but Allister lost his steamer, and I think his courage when he could not get another. His wife was dead, and the girl, giving up everything, came back here to help him. He carries the mails across and acts as ferryman, but I fancy there's a screw loose somewhere."

The tide had slackened when, seeing Allister's herring boat sliding across the sound, we rose to go. I was astonished to find only Miss Allister on board the craft, which was large and heavy. "Where is your father ? " Jack said, almost Neve:3ly. "It is a soldier's wind, fair both ways, and he is unwell again," said the girl; and I saw by the moonlight that she was avoiding my companion's eyes. Her face was very patient, and I felt sorry for her when she sat gripping the tiller while, with tall, black lugsail swaying athwart the silvery radiance, we slid across the channel. She seemed to know every eddy, and I saw that Jack was watching her admiringly. "Your father ought to send for one of the fishermen," he said. "This work is not fit for you." "Poor folks cannot always consider the fitness of things," said the girl, with a somewhat weary smile. She winced when Jack tendered her two :47.1.r coins, and as we clattered across the 'Angle he turned to me. "What do you think of Miss Northeote ? " said he.

"Very nice; and it is reported that she has several thousand pounds a-year of her own," I said. "Still, I don't fancy she thinks much of Carleton or me. She intimated that she preferred men of action, and there are folks who would envy your opportunities." Jack looked steadily at me. "There are," he said, "also folks who would resent your imper- tinent pleasantries." "Still, I understand you go to Major North- eote's pretty often," said I. "No doubt he is an interesting companion." Jack's face flushed a little, though he said nothing at all. He did not, however, cross the Sound for some little time, but I visited Major Northcote's house, as well as the ferry, and wondered whether it was because I was a friend of Jack's both ladies were gracious to me. Miss Northcote had, it seemed, been everywhere, and I sometimes wondered whether she had not seen too much, and was merely desirous of ascertain- ing whether Jack would provide a new sensation. It also struck me that Miss Allister's unspoilt human nature might be worth the other's several thousands a-year. Jack's thoughts were not apparent, if he had any, for he was working eighteen hours a day just then. At last, one .i:unny afternoon when I sat reading a technical journal on the beach beneath the ferry-house, Miss Allister approached me, and I laid it down for the pleasure of looking at her. "Here is an account of the quarries and rail- way, as well as its builder. It is evidently thought something of a feat," I said. The girl took the journal, and I saw the colour pale in her cheeks as she read. Her voice,Was also slightly uneven when she said: "Is this all authentic about Mr. Marston ? "
"Of course! He is a rising man, and was famous before he came here. Did you not know that?" said I.

"I did not," said the girl, and I saw her lips tremble as she abruptly turned away. I took the journal and flung it into the sea, then turned homewards, distinctly annoyed with myself. Here, I thought, was another case of the village maiden and Lord Burleigh though I was doubtful whether Jack had realised it yet. Other people had, however, for next night he strode into my room with his knuckles bleeding and dust upon his clothes. He also filled a large glass from the syphon before he turned to me. have been fighting. The man forced the quarrel on me," he said. "Who was he?" I said, in blank astonishment, for it was not often Jack made a fool of himself. "One of my own foremen, and a distant con- nection of Miss Allister's' " he said. "Now, for T:Teaven's sake listen, and give me good advice. C.he fellow waylaid me, and said if he couldn't have Helen Allister nobody of my description should *et her tglked about. He also said one or two insulting things, and when he struck Me I had to oblige him. We were both a little the worse for wear when we separated, bUt what worries me is that the man was right." "One question," said I. "What are your own feelings respecting Miss Allister ? " Jack's bronzed face grew darker. "We are fools, all of us, are we not ? " he said. "Some times I could drive Helen Allister's face from my recollection, and sometimes I couldn't; but I did my work as usual, and decided there would be time for my OVen affairs when my work was done. Now that fellow has opened my eyes, and I know there is only one woman in the world for me." "Then why don't you tell her so at once said L
"I was wondering whether it would not be better to wait until the railway was opened and I had more to offer her," said Jack, who was undoubtedly foolish in some respects. _ .

"It strikes me you have a trifle too much to offer, and have waited too long already," said .I. "Your prospects will not be worth much if she hears of your affair with the other fellow." It was next day when I came upon Jack sitting in his drawing office in a state of savage dejec- tion.

11e won't have me," he said, grimly. "Talked 40/me absurd rubbish about not dragging me down. It's curious, but I don't seem to care a brass button whether the confounded quarries are ever opened 'now." ‘Vhen i net visited the ferry-house Miss Allister did not seem in go_xl spirits, or especjally pleased to see me.- Her face was sadder than it had been, and the courage had vanished from her eyes. Jack in the meanwhile was toiling on stubbornly and moodily, .and I began to wonder what the end would be unless something beyond my contriving happened to set things straight. Somewhat strange to say, it • did one blustering evening when I strode down to the ferry-house to wait for Jack, who had gone across to consult with Northcote. The hills • were swathed in vapour. and 'wild bissts drivinc:down from their

unseen peaks smote tracks or trinteness across the sea. There was also a doleful wailing amidst the crags above me, while as I watched the current smoke beneath the squalls it struck me that it would be well if Jack delayed his cross- ing. The Sound of Craigmalin is not the place for a small craft with the wind against the stream.

Nobody seemed to notice me when I entered the house, but a hoarse voice was murmuring something in an inner room. Without thinking I pushed the door open, and then stood still in blank astonishment. Allister lay in disarrayed Arments staring at me without recognition, and .t did not need his raucous laugh to indicate what he was suffering from. The place reeked of ,vhisky, and I understood why Miss Allister carried the mails across the ferry. Turning away I met the girl in the passage, and signing me to follow her she went white to the lips. "You ,have ,seen him ? " she said, almost fiercely. "I have," said I. "May I offer you my respect- sympathy. Nobody else need know." The girl's face softened, and she seemed to choke back a sob. "It cannot be hidden much longer, but I should not like your friend to know until he has gone away," she said. "Perhaps I did wrong to hide it, but he is my father—and was always kind to me."

"You are a very brave girl, and if Jack is the man I think him I know what he will do when he hears," said I. A trace of colour crent into Miss Allister's lace. "Then you must not tell him. You dare not when I beg you not to," she said. I nodded solemnly, and feeling unequal to further discussion pointed towards the launch now dimly visible through the spray. "They are a little late." I said. _ _ _ _ _

The ifir glanced up at the black hill shoulders half seen in the mist, and down at the flying spray. The stream was pouring to windward through the Sound, and breaking horribly where it boiled over a rocky bottom, while the roar it made almost drowned the howling of the wind amidst the crags. I lost sight of the launch for some minutes, and when she lurched out of a black rain squall there was a stifled cry behind me.

"The engine has stopped," gasped the girl. "She will drive into the Skyoch Whirlpool or over the Malin Reef. We must take them off with the herring boat ! " I asked no questions, but dragged the dinghy down the shingle, and a squall drove us against the herring boat. We were scarcely on board her when the girl commenced to roll up the foot of the big tanned sail. "There is no time to lose. We must risk it with one reef down," she said. I had sailed a yacht of my own, but it was not without a struggle I set the thrashing sail. Then my heart was in my mouth as I east the moor- ings over as a squall came roaring down. The boat staggered and swayed down until the brine poured into her, then shaking the water from her she drove out into the spray. Springing aft I grasped the lugsail sheet, and looked doubtfully at Miss Allister, who sat high on the weather gunwale with little hands clenched on the tiller. She looked very slight and slender against the background of rushing water and whirling spray, and I guessed what would overtake us if her courage failed her. Still, she alone knew the swing and swirl of the current, which where it broke most furiously piled up a dangerous sea, and the boat was a big one with a ton or two of stone ballast inside her. Time and again, though Miss Allister dodged the worst of them, the seas poured deep across the little deck and then frothed into the well, while I glanced down at the water upon the ballast dubiously, and then at the wet rope in my hands. "Dare I get down and bale ? " I shouted. "Not for a moment," said the girl. "Slack the lugsheet now." The rope burnt my fingers, the reefed lugsail banged, and the boat plunged over in place of into a sea. There were a phalanx of them beyond it, and it was not the tumble of open water which runs regularly, but a foaming chaos where the current met the wind. We went through it, some- how, with the highest stones awash and the black lugsail dripping to the peak.. .
"There's the launch. Shall I haul the sheet again ? " I shouted in breathless gasps, and the girl pushed down her helm to lessen the pressure in the sail.
"Heaven send there's water over the Skyoch rock! Haul, and hold on through everything," she said.

I strained every muscle, and then hazarded a glance at her. The brine ran from her, and her wet hair whipped her face, but the little hands were still clenched bravely on the tiller. We went over the Skyoch, the boat swinging this way and that in defiance of her helm, while the sea poured into her. Then as she staggered out of the smother something black rolled amidst the spray, and with a crash of yielding timber we drove down upon the launch. Our shouts were probably inaudible, but three dripping objects caught our gunwale and scrambled out of the half-swamped launch. Miss Allister slipped from the tiller as one of them seized it, and it seemed only fitting that Jack should catch her. Then I slacked away the sheet, and we were flying homewards with the wind and the worst of the sea raging after us, while the boat made very fast travelling with the wild blast behind her. Presently somebody shouted, and then Carleton and I got the lugsail down and ran the boat well up on the ferry beach. It was Jack who sprang into the water to carry Miss Allister ashore, and I said to him:

"Use all your eloquence to-night, or never open your mouth again." Then, though Carleton seemed desirous of assisting, I passed Miss Allister down to Jack, and knowing the power of unspoilt human nature felt contented when he splashed ashore with her in his arms.
"You and I and Northcote's man will go on to the village. Miss Allister cannot look after us now," I said.
"The girl's splendid," said Carleton presently, with a whimsical smile. "Almost a pity it's my duty to marry money."
"It wouldn't maie any great difference if you hadn't to," said I.
It was some hours later when Jack strode exultantly into my room. "You can congratulate me, and I know all. She's even better than I thought her. Heaven bless her !" he said.

"It's a pity about the encumbrance," said L "Still, he is her father," said Jack, a trifle soberly. "I think I, see a way of getting over the difficulty. If she would do so much for a 'man of that kind, what will she do for me?'? This, I thought, was logical, and Miss Allister evidently found his suggestion workable, for when the quarries were opened she and Jack were married. Everybody came, including Miss Northcote and the quarrymen, and it was a year later when I met Carleton with the latter in London. He looked a trifle more lazily contented than he had done before, and his wife smiled as she noticed my mild astonishment. "James makes a very good husband. He is tranquil and does, not expect too much," she said.
I said I was pleased to hear it, and kept my thoughts to myself, because I knew two other people who had expected a good deal and obtained it.
ITIIR END. 1

THE WAY THROUGH THE WORLD. A dear little duck through an eggshell broke, It opened its eyes, and in duck language
_ spoke: "Quack quack," it murmured; "wherever am
I?" "Cluck, cluck," said the fussy old hen in reply. The dear little duck determined to take A walk through the world, and discoveries
make; Of what it was like, and of what it contained; Bo he went, and "Cluck, cluck," the old hen complained. The dear little duck encountered full soon A. dog, rso he stopped him and asked him a
boon; "Tell me, sir, how on this sunshiny day, "To walk through the world in the very beet
way." "My child," said he, with a fatherly air, "As you pass along you Must make it your

care; "To be kind to the small, and old, and weak, "To say a kind word whenever you speak; "Take the first turning that leads to, the right, "Don't leave it, and joy will be always in might." B. WARBURTON:
ASTS IN BACK GARDENS.

There are scores of people scattered about the country who have a mania for keeping minia- ture "Zoos." No matter how small the piece of ground at their disposal, they make a point of maintaining some kind of large animal, often of the most ferocious kind, as a sort of pet.

Some of these amateurs are popular and wealthy. Sir Henry Moss, for instance, keeps a variety of beasts, remarkably well looked after. Lions formed a part of his stock until lately, and very possibly at the present moment he could muster a lion or two.

There lives in -shire a country gentle- man, who keeps on his farm a pair of lions (well caged, of course), a trio of panthers, a brown-bear, a couple of wild asses, and numer- ous small fry. These animals require the undivided attention of a staff of keepers, and coat the owner a round sum, approaching £2O a week, for food and keep. Not long ago one of the panthers'escaped, and kept the country- side on pins and needles for three days, when it was shot in a field neai the owner's farm.

A lady, who resides near a city, has about a quarter of an acre of ground attached to her house, and on this plot she keeps a couple of leopards and a black bear. They are healthy beasts, with remalicable appetites for horse- flesh, and they are said to cost their owner more than the rest of her establishment every week. She also has a pair of zebras, not caged, but pastured in a well-fenced field. A physician keeps a full-grown lion in a small garden at the hack of his house, although his closest neighbours do not suspect the fact. It must be a singularly quiet lion, but its exist- enoe there is unquestionable. He feeds it cn butcher's meat---not common horseflesh—and cleans out its cage himself every Saturday. He is probably the most eccentric of all amateur menagerie keepers. In all there are about a couple of hundred people in the country who go in for keeping wild beasts, and they are to be reckoned with by the wild beast dealers. We hope the craze may not become too widespread.

BOUQUETS. Buttercups and daisies, Violets and may, Pimpernels and cowslips, Make a sweet bouquet. Not a rose among them, Nought the garden yields; Yet a lot of beauty Taken from the fields. Gathered in the sunshine. Through the happy -hours; What a sweet bouquet, dears, Made of simple flowers! Patience and forgiveness, Kindness to the, weak,. Willing in our labour All the happy week. NO exalted actions, Striving after praise;. Yet a lot of beauty From life's lowly ways. Gathered through the day, dear, By the heart that heeds;. What a sweet biniquet, dear, Made of simple deeds. • ELIZABETH STOCKS.

div.head: SUMMER'S LODGING.
div.p: A SUMMER'S LODGING.

Two summers ago a couple of tomtits built their nest and reared their young in the letter- box of the Uttoxeter 'Union Workhouse. Later the birds took their departure, and the nest was cleared out and destroyed. Nothing more was seen of them until last summer, when the same Mrs. Tomtit began to build her nest in exacfly the same place. The home was soon completed, and to show the activity of the bird it is enough -to state that within a fortnight the nest was built and a collection of six eggs laid. The lettere continued to be delivered in the box, and sometimes completely covered the mother, who took no notice whatever, except to shake her tail by way of appreciation when they were taken off her back. W. ELLIOTT.

WILLIE'S SUM. Willie laid his pencil down, And put his books away; And with a sad and peevish frown He hurried out to play. But as he ran, the blackbird's song, From poplars in. the lane, Rang out, "You know that sum was wrong, And should be done again." Yet Willie heeded not the sound, Pretended not to hear, Till trees, and hills, and all around Kept singing in his ear: "It's no use, Willie; trust us, do! You can't enjoy the fun Until the task that's set for you Is well and justly done." Then in a sad and sorry state, He homeward turned amain; Took up his pencil and his slate, And worked the sum again. This time the answer wasn't wrong, And as to play he went, '.His conscience sang an altered song,. Which made his heart content. DAISY STOcKS.

div.head: AN UP-TO-DATE DEFENCE.
div.p: AN UP-TO-DATE DEFENCE.
"We propose to show, gentlemen of the jury," said counsel for the defence, "that it is impossible, for the defendant to have com- mitted this crime. _ _

"In the first place, we will prove that the defendant was nowhere near the scene of the crime at the time the crime was committed. "Next we will offer the indisputable testi- mony of persons who saw defendant on the spot, and who did not see the defendant com- mit the crime. _ _ .

"We will show that no poison was found in the body of the deceased. "Not only that, but we will prove that it was put there by the prosecution in this case. "We will furthermore show that the deceased committed suicide.
"And last, but not least, we will prove, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that the deceased is not dead, _ .
"In view of all which corroborative facts, gentlemen of the jury, we respectfully ask or an acquittal."

A student undergoing examination in the principles of mechanics, was asked, "Why will not a pin stand on its point?" He returned the following answer: "In the finst' place, a point is defined by Euclid as that which hath no parts, •and no magnitude, and how can ,a pin stand on that which hath no parts and no magnitude? In the second place, it will, if you stick it in hard enough."

A somewhat similar story. is told of a well- known Q.C. Observing that his wife always delayed ten or twelve minutes before she came down to dinner, and being loth. to lose so much precious time daily, he commenced the c4.maro,:.tion of a legal work, which he prosecuted tally I,vlAle he was thus kept waiting. The result wars, at the end of fifta:n years, a book (if published it would have made three gigantic volumes), which was regarded by the Q.C. and his friends as a monument of indus- try, and as a standing protest against those who idly fritter away time.. Unfortunately, however, the Q.C. has not been able to discover any one willing to publish the tremendous volumes..
He become e a very angry man indeed when any one talks to him about the utilisation of odd moments.

It was- a hot Sunday afternoon, and during the sermon a man In a smOck frock, sitting hi the gallery over the clock, every now and then leaned over to see the time. After some time the irritated preicher could stand it no longer, and addressing himself to the gallery, he. exclaimed: "I beg to inform that man who con-- tinues to look at the clock that it is twenty-- three minutes past four. and I shall have done, ray dreary sermon in a minute or two." "If you please. sir," came the unexpected answer from the gallery, "I warn't a bit tired o' your sermon; but the cows mann milked."

ODDFELLOWS' ANNUAL HANDICAP.

The fifth annual handicap promoted by the "Prince of Wales " Lodge took place at the Brooklands Hotel, Lovely-lane, last Saturday in the presence of a large crowd of spectators. The entries numbered 50. The weather was favourable and the green and surroundings were a credit to Bro. James Earle, the proprietor. The games were keenly contested and in the final 3. Howard defeated D. Bromley, who has twice previously been in the final, by 13-12. The winner thus holds the Silver Cup given by Mr. A. H. Crosfleld, M.P., for twelve months and also wins the beautiful Gold Medal also given by Mr. A. H. Crosfield. Sixteen other prizes were awarded. The committee who had charge of the arrangements were : Bros. T.P. Brathhaw (chairman),H. Maddock, T. Reddish, J. Massey, W. King, E. Clayton, John Willett and G. F. Freeman ,(secretary). Bro. V. Whitnam officiated as handicapper and clerk of the green. The prizes will be presented at a Social to be held later. The Grand Master and Deputy Grand Master were not able to be present owing to the Odd- fellows Sports at Cadishead.

THE CEMETERY INN BOWLING CLUB. LADIES' MAIN.

This is doubtless an age when the members of the fair sex enter to a large extent into the sports of men, which a few years ago might • have been thought rather unbecoming and quite ont of place, but the days of such thoughts seem to have died a natural death, as was clearly exemplified on Thursday, on the Green of the Cemeterrlnn Bowling Club, when 50 ladies presented themselves to compete for valuable prizes on the occasion of their Annual Main. This is about the third occasion on which the green has been reserved for the members of the fair sex, and there is not the slightest doubt that the innovation has become extremely popular and the annual event is always looked forward to with a large amount of interest and expectation. Several of the ladies showed especial aptitude in their knowledge of the mysteries of the "finger and thumb peg," and some of the woods would have done credit to the male section. The winner was Miss Higham who played exceptionally well throughout, and in the final beat Mrs. Cottam by 7-1. Tea was provided for the participants in the main, in the Billiard room, the tables being very tastefully decorated with plants and flowers. Mr. and Mrs. Allison provided an excellent repost,and full-justice was done to it by the "lady trundlers." Unfortunately the clerk of the weather proved to be a litttle ungenerous,as almost immediately after tea rain began to fall, and continued incesssantly until the happy gathering dispersed. Narrow Escape from Dissection Alive. Sir,—The London "Daily Express" of July 24th contains the following from its Vienna correspondent under date of July 23rd :—" Johann Kovacs, a railway station porter at Bihar, in Hungary, had yesterday a narrow escape of being dissected alive. Two days ago be fell down unconscious while at work, and was taken to the hospital. The doctors pronounced him dead,and a post mortem was decided on, for which all prepara- tions were made, the bddy being put on the dissecting table, ,when a lecture was dslivered over it to the students before the body was opened. At the first prick of the knife, Kovacs awoke with a start and as soon as he realised his •position, endeavoured to assault the surgeon who held the dissecting knife. He had to be forcibly restrained by the other doctors." The above adds another to the already long list of cases clearly showing the difficulty which even duly qualified medical men often experience in distinguish- ing between real and apparent death. In an exhaustive work on this subject, entitled "Premature Burial and how it may be prevented " by William Tebb, F.R.C.S., and the late Colonel E. P. Vollum of the United States Army, many analogous cases to the above are recorded. Indeed, on page 277, I read: "There is scarcely a dis- secting room that has not some traditional story handed down of subjects restored to life after being deposited within its walls." In view of these facts, such subjects as the scientific study of the various species of death counterfeit, and the effecting of such reforms as will safeguard everyone against such dangers as dissection, cremation, burial or any other mode of disposal before the actual fact of death, must be seen to be of paramount importance.—Yours faithfully, J. WEST. Bradford-on-Avon, August stn, 1907.

div.head: DEATH OF COLONEL RIDGWAY, J.P.
div.p: DEATH OF COLONEL RIDGWAY, J.P.

A painful sensation was created in Warrington and district by the news of the death of Colonel John Clare Ridgway, who passed away at his residence, Daresbury Lodge, on Wednesday evening, after a very brief illness. The deceased gentleman was at business last • Friday, and so ' late as Tuesday morning he appeared to be quite well. The same day he had a sudden seizure and Dr. Bowers was -called in but death ensued on Wednesday. Colonel Ridgway, who was 67 years of age, had for many years been closely identified with the commercial life of Warrington and commanded the respect and affection of a wide circle. He was of a kindly, unassuming disposition and no one who was associated with him in any work could fail to appreciate his many good qualities. Colonel Ridgway was proud to call himself aLancashire man, having been born at Strangeways Hall, a building which occup:ed the site of the now famous prison. The Ridgway family have, however, for some ten generations lived in Cheshire, their remains having been laid to rest at Knntsford, some in the old church- yard, _ and some hi the new. Colonel Ridgway lost his father when he was only ten years of age. His mother was a Warrington lady, and was the daughter of Captain Clgre. As Colonel Ridgway used to spend all his holidays with his grandfather at War- ringon he had a very long connection with the town, coming to reside here permanently in the year 1867. He entered into the business carried on by his grandfather at Warrington and Sankey Bridges as a slate and building merchant, and ultimately the firm took its present title of Clare and Ridgway. For many years Colonel Ridgway was the sole partner in the firm, with which he was personally connected during the whole of his residence in Warrington. For the last two years the concern has been a limited company. Colonel Ridgway was ~ rhaps best known to the majority of Warringtonians reason of the prominent part which he took in the Volunteer movement. Before coming to Warrington he served as a Volunteer, but he did not rejoin the force until 1880 when he became associated • with the Ist Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. He took the warmest interest in the work of the battalion and ultimately became its colonel. He did all he could to encourage the men to make the corps thoroughly efficient and his efforts were attended with gratifying success. He was genuinely esteemed by the men under his command, who recognized in him a true friend. During the South African campaign he was largely instrumental in raising the active service contingents which went to the Cape. He was not unmindful of the needs of those whom the soldiers and volunteers had to leave behind, and his work on the Relief Com- mittee which raised £7,260 for the dependents was truly a labour of love. He was the recipient of an illuminated address bearing his own portrait and those of other prominent helpers, and worded as follows :—" Presented to Colonel Ridgway, J.P., by the Transvaal War Relief Committee for his valuable .services on the committee appointed to raise funds for the relief of the wives and families of Reservists and Volunteers on active service in South Africa." On „ retiring from the Volunteers a few years ago,Colonel Ridgway was succeeded by Colonel Edelsten. It may safely be said that his interest in the move- ment continued unabated and he was always a strong advocate of generous treatment being .meted out to Volunteers by the authorities. He was a strong believer in some form of compulsory military training. Colonel Ridgway was appointed a Justice of the Peace for the Borough by the Crown in the year 1889, and amongst other public offiees which be filled were the following': —Vice-President of -the Musical Society, one of the Ccmmissioners of income, property and land tax for the Bucklow Division of Cheshire, and a trustee of the Blue Coat School. In politics he was a Conservative, but he never took an active part in party warfare. He leaves a widow, two sum and one daughter, with whom the deepest sym- pathy is felt in their bereavement. One of the sons is a lieutenant in the S. Staffs. Regt. and is at present in India. The funeral take; place at Daresbury church at 12 moon to-day (Saturday). MAGISTERIAL REFERENCES. Before commencing the ordinary business at the Borough Court on Friday m*aing, the Mayor said it was his painful duty to have to express. the deep ir regret of the Magistrates of the Borough at the death. of Colonel Ridgway, one of the oldest members belong- ing to that Bench. The late Colonel took an aCtive part on the Bench for a long number of years, until be removed to Cheshire. He (the Mayor) knew Colonel Ridgway as an honest and upright man. The town had lost one of the oldest inhabitants, and one of the golden links belonging to the old families of the town. He was sure that those in camp, as well as those present, who were associated with the deceased, would receive the news with the deepest regret. Mr. Browne,on behalf of the solicitors practising in that court associated himself with the remarks of the Mayor and,said he could speak of the Colonel as being an upright true and honest man. He remembered the time when Colonel Ridgway used to sit with Mr. Moreland. Crosfield. Mr. Browne said he 'sincere' sympathised with the bereaved and sorrowing family.

div.head: SCENE IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.
div.p: SCENE IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.
ROYAL COURT THEATRE. The Re-opening Play. " BESIDE THE BONNIE BRIER BUSH."

The transformed Royal Court Theatre, the structural - details of which were described in our last issue, was opened on Monday evening with a demonstration of public enthusiasm which augurs well for its future success. The proprietors, Messrs. Johgson and Potter, hit the public taste to a nicety in selecting" Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush "as the play wherewith to re-open the new building which, has, phosnix-like,arisen from the ashes of the disastrous fire of last Christmas morning. The new Royal Court Theatre is alike a credit to the town and its proprietors, and from the architect downwards through all concerned in carrying out his ideas congratulations may be offered freely and without stint. Soon after five o'clock queues extending as far as Briege-street in one direc- tion and to Cairo-street in the other, began to form, and the raising of the curtain disclosed a house packed to its fullest capacity with an audience delighted equally with the comforts of the theatre as with the play itself. ' Mr. William Mollison's company dealt with the dramatised version of lan Maclaren's prose fiction with that perfect smoothness which comes of repetitions running into the centuries. The play embodies a 4uite orthodox moral lesson and some strong situations though one is left with the feeling that the author has not made the most of these as they affect some of the principal characters. The part of Lord Flay for instance —one pervaded by a sense of perfect rectitude in conduct —is singularly cold-shouldered in the concluding scene,in which the unanswered question arises why a nobleman, so unimpeachable in speech and behaviour yet con- tinually under suspicion, does not in the denouement assert himself in strong terms against the father-in-law who has so consistently wronged him. But the story has a powerful old-world charm about it, and in the portrayal of its broad feature of the all-absorbing parental solicitude of a widowed father for an only daughter, one is carried above and beyond criticism of detail. Mr. Mollison's impersonation of the principal part of Lachlan Campbell is so thoroughly imbued with human instincts as to carry conviction in every phase of the long gamut of emotion on which it is played, and, supported as M. Mollison is by a most capable oompany,the piece has, each evening run its length with a naturalness which has been the delight of nightly crowded houses. Between the acts there have been many calls before the curtain during the week and the applause has been unmistakeably enthusiastic. On Monday Mr. Mollison took advantage of one of the "calls" to address a few words of congratulation to the proprietors and to the audience upon having such a beautiful theatre in their midst. It was, he said, a pleasure to play in such a theatre, and he could not say how pleased he was to have been asked to open it. It was a great change for the better from the place he acted in once before—about sixteen years ago. He acted the stock season then, and it was there he met his wife, who was playing the leading business, as she was that night. (Applause.) He therefore looked with a great deal of affection upon Warrington. They ought all to be very proud of the building Messrs. Johnson and Potter had provided, and they ought to feel proud of such an architect as Mr. Smith. (Applause.) One thing/the had praised that night specially was the dressing-room accommodation. As a rule the dressing-rooms were left to the last, but in this ' case the artistes had been given commodious and beauti- fully fitted rooms. All he had got to say now was "God bless them, and prosper their beautiful theatre."' (Applause.) At the conclusion of the play Mr. Mollison was again constrained to make a speech. Stepping to the front he thanked the audience on behalf of himself and his company for their kindly, thoughtful and intel- lectual appreciation of their efforts. He hoped they would look over any little shortcomings in the play that night, because given in a new theatre, everything was necessarily a little in the rough. (Applause.) Mr. Potter also took the opportunity of thanking the audience on behalf of himself and his partner for their hearty appreciation of their efforts to cater for the entertainment of the public, and hoped it would not be the last time they would have a" house" of that size. (Applause.) He thanked Mr. Smith, the architect, for his work in connection with the erection of that build- ing.—Mr. Smith replied, and praised the efforts of all the contractors, who had united in doing their best to erect a theatre which would be a credit to the town. ' —ln response to calls, Mr. Johnson appeared on the stage. He said there were several important London productions the proprietors would like to have obtained during the present season, but tours were arranged so far ahead that they had been unable to get them. How- ever, they had arranged for a splendid series of com- panies to appear, but after the present season they would be able to secure those they had been obliged to miss for the present. The support the public would ' kindly give them would help the proprietors in the direction of bringing better-class companies than had ever appeared in Warrington. (Applause.) With these latter sentiments the editorial "we" is

- in complete accord. Warrington has now a playhouse such as it has long and patiently waited for, and,granted that it is conducted upon right lines, as we are assured it will be, there is no reason why it should not prosper commercially in ministering to the reasonable enjoy- ment of thousands of our townspeople. We wish the enterprising proprietors of the Royal Court Theatre a full measure of success in their new venture.
