div.head: Examiner, Saturday August 10, 1907,
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday August 10, 1907,

Unless the conditions quickly improve, says a corres- pondent writing on Thursday, it is feared that the Sonth Lancashire Brigade will have to carry away with it the impression that not much good in the matter of weather is to be expected from Llanberis. A. kind of fatalism seems to hover around these mountains. They scarcely showed their beads during the last two days. Rain began to fall heavily on Wednesday evening, and continued unceasingly all through the night till about nine o'clock on Thursday morning. It also blew fiercely at times, but the tents withstood the elements well, and such is the nature of the ground that, with the exception bf beaten tracks, it had dried up in a remark- able manner by noon. Colonel Edelsten, of thc Ist. South Lancashire Regiment announced the death of his predecessor, Colonel Ridgway, the sad news being received with deep regret. After some battalion drills in the morning, the whole brigade were in the afternoon exercised in route march- ing. Four miles of the road up the pass was chosen for the march, and the battalions fell in in the follow- ing order :-Ist South Lancashire, 2nd South Lanca- shire, 3rd Liverpool. and 6th Liverpool. They were accompanied by their respective bands, and the Cyclist Company constituted an advance guard. Extending for nearly a mile, the column presented an imposing appear- ance. An average pace of three and a half miles per hour was registered. The outward journey was per- formed in fine weather, but during the last hour of the return march rain came down in torrents, the whole valley being enveloped in a black pall of clouds. The men suffered some discomfort from the absence of great coats, but their zest was in no way damped. There was every prospect of another continuous downpour overnight, and the men of the 6th entertained hopes of seeing the Channel Fleet coming up on the next flood. Torrents of rain fell during Thursday night. Many tents had small rivers of water running through them, and they were abandoned, the men sleeping in halls in Llanberis. Trenches like miniature redoubts were cut round the tents to drain off as much water as

possible. Yesterday the sun came out, the camps soon present- ing a quaint appearance, ropes being suspended from tent to tent on which trousers, tunic shirts, and blankets were hung to dry. To-day, weather permitting, the brigade contemplate a march to Carnarvon. The centre attraction for the Volunteers when off duty is undoubtedly the Y.I.V.C.A. tent. Every night it is crowded with men, some of whom are writing letters, some reading, while others are singing: Not only can they write letters, for which stationary is pro- vided gratis, but they can post them in the tent. Refreshments are provided, and everything that can be desired is done for the men. On Wednesday the famous band of the 6th V.B. King's (Liverpool Regiment) played a few selections, which were thoroughly enjoyed. Captain J. T. Clarke presided, and was supported by Lieut. Paris. The band, with its energetic bandmaster, is to be congratulated upon the splendid pieces which were rendered, and one was not surprised to hear the men giving three hearty cheers at the close to the chairman' bandmaster, and Lieut. Paris, for all were delighted with such an unexpected treat. THE RETURN.
The Warrington Volunteers will return to-morrow (Sunday), and are expected to arrive in town at about one o'clock.

div.head: VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: THE VOLUNTEERS.
CAMP AT LLANBERIS.

This week our local Volunteers—or to give them their full title, the members of the lsit V.B. (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment —have been encamped at Llanberis in North Wales. When it became known that this picturesque spot had been selected, there was general satisfaction in the battalion, for the change is a welcome one after the series of encampments at such a remote place as Salisbury Plain, admirable though the latter may be from the point of view of military manceuvring. Llanberis is a delightfully situated village, almost on the slopes of Snowdon, and is not very far from Carnarvon which is a popular resort. This year the encampment is only for a week instead of for a fortnight, the period allowed of late years. The Volunteers left Warrington on Sunday morning, their departure being witnessed by a large number of townspeople. When the men had assembled on the Town Hall lawn the scene was an imposing one, and the selections played by the band, under the direction of Bandmaster Richardson, gave great pleasure. Two special trains had been engaged and, leaving Warrington at about eleven o'clock, the Volunteers arrived at Llanberis at three in the afternoon. Dinner was served and after- wards blankets, &c., were issued and preparations were made for the first night under canvas. Although the weather during the week has no -been of the most favourable des- cription, it has not ,interfered much with the work of the camp and some exceedingly interesting move- ments have been carried out. We have no doubt that the men will have benefited by thein stay in one of the most beautiful districts of North Wales.

div.head: LIFE AT LLANBERIS.
div.p: LIFE AT LLANBERIS.
Details of the Week's Operations.

On Sunday the usual Sabbatical stillness of the picturesquely-situated village of Llanberis was broken by the arrival of a sufficiently large body of men in uniform to outnumber the normal population of the place. The invasion was that of tha South Lancashire Brigade, consisting of four battalions, which travelled from its different headquarters in special trains. The camp iS pitched on two level fields of 50 acres in extent on each side of the main road, and in close proximity to the station of the London and North-Western Rail- way. . .

Seven or eight special trains were requisitioned to convey the various battalions to their destination. The first arrived about six in the morning, and the remainder came at intervals up to bait-past three in the afternoon, when there was a lull till eight o'clock, when the last train discharged its freight. One or two ef the battalions, however, seemed to experience difficulty in getting stores and baggage carted from the station. There was a dearth of carters, and in some quarters this was attributed to the objection of local teamowners to Sunday labour. A taste of nature in its most angry moods was experi- enced by the advance parties of the brigade who were quartered on the ground on Saturday night. A storm of wind and rain swept over the camp demolishing the canteen of the 6th King's (Liverpool Regiment) and playing havoc with the sergeants' messroona and a few other tents. On the field on the lower side of the road, which practically adjoins the lake, the ground became very wet and sloppy, but as the day advanced the warm rays of the sun laid bare the summits of the surrounding mountains and dried up the camping ground in a remarkably short time. The brigade consists of four battalions. At the far end of the field on the upper side of the road are encamped the 6th V.8.K.L.R., who arrived by two trains in the afternoon. The marching in state of this battalion with the Isle of Man contingent was 649 men. Next on the same field come the 3rd K.L., the strength of the battalion being 306. Next to the road will be found the camp of the 2nd South Lancashire, from St. Helens, which consists of thirty officers and 750 men. By themselves, on the other side of the road, are the Ist South Lancashire, from Warring- ton, having 760 of all ranks. There are in this battalion seventy-five mounted infantry and a. cyclist company of seventy-two men. Their officers are Lieut.- Colonel Edelston (cbmmanding), Major J. D. Fair- dough, Captain and Acting-Adjutant A. G. Roberts, Captains A. B. Layton, C. Cary, R. Smith, P. N. Avery (commanding mounted infantry), and H. Owen, Lieuts. R. H. Lapage, J. D. Picton, and J. D. Boumphrey, Seoond-Lieuts. G. Fairclough (commanding cyclist company) and M. Woods Surgeon-Major Adams, and Captain and Quartermaster Potter. It may be added that this is the first time that the Ist Battalion has brigaded with the South Lancashire, as they formerly formed part of an Army Corps. Colonel J. H. Verschoyle is. the brigadier command- ing, and he is accompanied by Brigade-Major Cart- wright, the transport officer for the brigade being Colonel Carruthers.

Monday's fine weather helped the battalions to form a very favourable impression of their camping ground and its surroundings. They were at the same time reminded by the hilly character of the manceuvring ground that Volunteering in Snowdonia is not a mere picnic. General Sir Francis Bennett, K.C.8., who is the chief in command of the Western District, inspected the various battalions before breakfast.

At 9.15 the camp turned out and marched up the slopes of Eilian and Snowdon to the ground at Cwmdwythwch, which has an area of about four square miles. Here General Bennett visited the battalions and watched them go through their drills, which chiefly comprised company drills and extended order movement. In some parts the ground was boggy, and rendered the experience of the mounted'men and cyclists the reverse of pleasant, though they good-humouredly regarded it as in the day's work. By two o'clock all the men were back again, as were also the cyclists' corps, who numbering close upon 200, had movements of their own in the neighbourhood of Llanrug. An hour later General Bennett inspected the men and their kits. The camp proved a great holiday attraction on Sunday to the inhabitants of Llanberis and people from a distance, the fine music discoursed by the band of the Ist South Lancashire being especially appreciated. On Tuesday the Brigade carried out a scheme of mountain warfare which was somewhat unexpectedly decided upon the previous day by General Sir Francis Burbett, commanding the Western Division. During the operations the weather proved most favourable, which was fortunate, in view of tbe hard nature of the ground and the long distance to be traversed. i The commanding officers of the various battalions met the brigadier, Colonel Verschoyle, on the parade ground of the 6th King's (Liverpool Regiment) shortly after nine o'clock, when the orders for attack and distribution of troops were issued. At the same time the units fell in on their private parade grounds, and each man carried thirty rounds of blank cartridge. The general idea was that the 2nd South Lancashire, representing a force of Afridis, were in. occupation of the western slopes of Snowdon, and collecting for the purpose of raiding the town of Llanberis, the remainder of the brigade being directed to move out to attack them and clear the surrounding hills. The boggy land to be encountered on part of tbe ground precluded the mounted infantry and the cyclist corps from participating in the operations, and they were exercised independently under their own commanders. The invaders were found to be holding a position on the Tryfan Ridge in very strong force, the main portion being in the rear. The Ist South Lancashire formed to the left or the line, and the Gbh Icing's held the right, while the 3rd South Lancashire were in reserve in the centre, and _were noti brought into action till the last moment. The enemy came along the ridge and into the valley, gradually driving back the defence posts. They were, however, outflanked by the 6th, whose flanking movement was prolonged further to the right to the river Arbbu, with the result that the position of the enemy became untenable, being also attacked in front and on their right flank by the Ist South Lancashire,l and they were obliged to retire about twelve o'clock. The 3rd South Lancashire was advanced by the brigadier up to the Halfway House, and the "cease fire" sounded , at 1.30.

Efforts were made to impart as much realism as possible to the operation, and they proved highly suc- cessful, the enemy being split up into groups, each group carrying banners and indulging in war cries which resounded through the hills and caused no little merri- ment. The ease with which the men moved over the crags was marvellous, and they also covered the ground at an excellent pace. _ _

At the conclusion of the operations General Burnett 1 and all the officers assembled at the Half-way House, when a report of the movements of each battalion was ' supplied by the respective commanding officers. The• inspecting officer expressed his great pleasure at the ' way in which the defence was performed by the let South Lancashire and the 6th King's. This he regarded , as being all the more creditable in view of the sudden- 1 ness with which the scheme had been sprung upon the! brigade. They had demonstrated clearly what they ' could accomplish in active service at short notice. Asked by one of the officers if he considered that the Volunteers were fit for active work, General Burnett , said that he most certainly was of that opinion as he,! was perfectly satisfied with what he had seen. It may ! be added that the men on their pert were exceedingly keen on the work, and their endurance is proved by the fact that none fell out.

After their hard day's work on Tuesday the South Lancashire Battalions on Weinesday returned, under their respective commanders, to the more general routine of camp life. The cyclists and the mounted infantry had independent schemes of operations of their own. The camping ground at Llanberts has proved all that could be desired, being convenient to the manceuyring ground, which covers over twelve squsre miles.

div.head: " CITIE OF THELWALL." Something of its Ancient History.
div.p: THE " CITIE OF THELWALL." Something of its Ancient History.

Some interesting details of the early history of Thelwall were given by the Rev. W. J. Stanton in the course of a sermon at the village church on Sunday. The rev, gentleman has just presented a tablet as a memorial to Edward the Elder, the founder of the " citie of Thelwall," and to commemorate the coronation of King Edward VII, after an interval of a thousand years. The memorial has been placed on the south walls of the church. Speaking from the text "A thousand years "(Pa. xc. 4), the preacher pictured the country and Thelwall district as it was in the early part of the tenth century -about 150 years before the Norman Conquest. He supposed the greatest contrast between the scene then and what it is now would be in the wilderness of the land,the want of cultivation,and the fewness of the inhabitants. All to the south of them, he said, there would be a vast forest of great trees with, here and there, a clearing containing a few huts of wattle and daub, the homes of husbandmen or charcoal burners. Now and then the traveller would reach a larger collection of houses with a church of stone or, likely, plaster—a mill, and a certain amount of trade; or again, there might be a hermit's cell amid the trees or a monastery very different from the great abbeys of later times, but still a plae,a, of refuge, of hospitality and civilization where religion and learning went out to all the countryside. For the most part, however, the way would be lonely, even dangerous by rough forest roads, infested with wolves and other dangerons beasts and bands of lawless men. The wayfarer would often need to pray the petition of the English Church Litany of those days: "From Danes and all other savage men, from wolves and all other savage beasts, good Lord, deliver us !" To the north would be the Mersey in its winding course, only far wider than we ever knew it, stretching out over the meadows in marshes and bogs especially on the north bank, where it formed a vast morass many miles in width, the forerunner of the moss of our own days, with pools of water and deep dykes and the remains of groat trees making the whole almost impassable. This must have extended nearly to Manchester, but just here, where the land rises somewhat, the moss would become confined in a narrower bed, making a passage easy, and so there' would be need of a fortress if there was danger from the north. And it was from the north that-there ' was danger to the English. There were the Celts of Strathclyde—the British kingdom extending from Glasgow to the Ribble ; there were the Sorthumbrian Dane; who owned the couutry to the north-east, and had extended their power right across England to the Irish Sea. It might be that Thelwall had existed long before that time as a frontier fortress of the kingdom of Mercia. which occupied all the centre of England, but they first heard of it after the independent kings of Mercia had passed away and all this part o f the country was under the rule of the West Saxon kings ' from the south. That was why in the tablet there was just below the crown a shield bearing a dragon which was the emblem of the West Saxons. Then, in the autumn of 923„ there came to Thelwall a great king—Edward, son of Alfred the Great—and ordered the place to be built (which looked as though it may have existed before), made strong and garrisoned. for the times were troublons and the king desired a stronghold in which he and his army might pass h e winter, and from whence he could attack his enemies, and we read that be went out from Thelwall and took Manchester, which had been captured by the Danes of Northumberland. They might be proud that their founder was the first of their kings to bear a name so great and famous in history, and certainly he was not the least illustrious bearer of it. If he we.; not so wonderfully clever as his father in the arts of peace he was at any rate as brave and good a soldier, and under him England attained to greatness such as it had never reached before among the nations of Europe, and at home the whole nation was united under one Sovereign, Nor not only did Edward become the one king over all the English, but the princes of Wales and Scotland. Northumberland and Strathclyde, acknowledged him as their superior and did him homage, so that he became the first Sovereign Lord of all the island.

That land would be raised, levelled, and improved, and would in coming years be a valuable asset. By the Bridge- water Canals Act owners of mines and minerals %ander the Leigh branch of that Canal were empowered to work the same whilst the Company's interests were safeguarded. They got from the mineowners guaranteed amount of toll traffic on the Bridgewater Canal for a certain number of years. The passing of the bill through Parliament had cost them nothing.

div.head: SHIP CANAL, Enconraging Story of Continued Progress. THE WARRINGTON JUDGMENT.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL, Enconraging Story of Continued Progress. THE WARRINGTON JUDGMENT.

The forty-fourth ozdinary general meeting of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held in the Memorial Hall, Manchester' on Thursday. Mr. J. K. Bythell, chairman of the Company, 'presided. There was a full attendance of directors.

Mr. Bythell, in moving the adoption of the report said it was grat;fyinE,, to observe that the figures again indicated progress. (Hear, hear.) The weight of seaborne merchandise imported and exported by means of the Ship Canal amounted to 2,271,583 tons, against 2,112.813 tons during the first half of 1906—an increase ,of 158,770 tons. The receipts from the Ship Canal department were £248,833, against £233,176— increase £15,157 ; whilst the expenditure was £134,708, or £827 more. The increased expenditure would have been greater but for the fact that the amount expended on the repair of the Liam Lock was £6,000 less than in the corresponding half of last year. The principal items on the expenditure side which I showed an increase were—traffic expenses, working of locks and swing bridges, compensation to workmen &c., , rates and taxes, and law charges. The net result Of the working of the Ship Canal department was a profit of £113,625. against £99,215—an increase of £14,330. The i half-year's profit or, the Bridgewater department I amounted to £17,408—a decrease of £B5O. The receipts showed an increase, but there had been a much heavier lexpenditure on wages and boat hire. - THE WARRINGTON JUDGMENT. He dared say they had seen that the law lords had reversed the decision of the Court of Appeal in the ; Warrington case, and had restored Lord Justice Byrne's ' judgment, which, to use his own words was to the effect that the depth of eight feet means eight feet of water beloß the low-water level of spring tides, and does not mean eight feet below any permanent datum. "We can do nothing," Mr. Bythell said. "but loyally ob,y this decision of the highest authority in the land. We shall continue to endeavour to do our duty and spend, as we have done since Mr. Justice Byrne's judgment, a very much larger amount of money than before that date. lam glad to be able to tell you that the amount S VALLOWING MATCH-HEADS. placed to reserve in the three or four years will be absolutely sufficient to cover all claims and costs." div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Vaccination Fees Reduced.

A meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr. W. Houghton presiding. There were also present :—Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Simpson, Miss Broadbent, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, J. Billinge, W, Gill, W. C. Brooks, W. Furness, R. Bolton,S. Davies, A. Brooks, J. Cook, G. Mather, W. Flanagan, T. Ritchie, E. L. Bent, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), A. Wright tsuperintend- ent of Cottage Homes.)

PENKETII AND REGISTRATION. The CLERK said he had received a letter from the Clerk to tbe Parish Council of Penketh stating that there was no office for registration in that parish. He had replied that it was a question for the Registrar General.
INFECTIOUS DISEASES. THE MAINTENANCE OF PATIENTS.

The CLERK reported that he had interviewed the Town Clerk with regard to the question of payment for the maintenance of patients sent from the Work- house to the Corporation infectious diseases hospital. He had agreed with the Town Clerk that if the Corpora- tion still thought they should be paid, the question should be referred to the Local Government Board. Since the interview he had received a letter from the Town Clerk stating that the Health Committee had agreed to refer the question of liability to the Local Govern- ment Board and asking him (Mr. Sutton) to prepare the statement of the Guardians' case. It was suggested that the best plan would be to send the two statements togrthe!r..

Mr. EvaNs said the Health Committee thought the course suggested would be the best solution. The CHAIRMAN : It has been a more or less vexed question for some time. Mr. EVANS : If both the statements go together none of us can complain. The Board agreed to refer the matter to the Local Government Board.
VACCINATION. SMALLER FEES FOR THE DOCTORS.

rhe special committee appointed to deal with vaccination fees submitted the following resolution : "Recommended that the contracts with the public vaccinators be amended by the substitution of a fee of three shillings for that of five shillings in respect of each successful vaccination performed within the area of the County Borough of Warrington, and the sub- stitution of a fee of three shillings and sixpence for that of five shillings in respect of each successful vaccination performed within the other vaccination areas within the Union."No further reduction of the fees was proposed. The Clerk was instructed to send a copy of this notice to each public vaccinator, with an intimation that the Board would consider any observation he might desire to make to them thereon. The CLERK read a letter from Dr. Sephton stating that he hoped the Guardians would consider his district as being very different from any other in the Union, as it had a large area and a small and scattered population necessitating long distances to be covered in visiting the houses. His vaccination fees on the present scale did not amount to £2O a year. A fee of 2s. 6d. woull be very little for the long distances he had to travel. The CLERK said Dr. Sephton's was the largest area with the smallest amount of fees in the 'Union. The average sum paid to him during the past four years was £2B, but that included a year when there was an out- break of small-pox. Last year his fees amounted to £2O. Dr. Valentine, of Earlestown, wrote stating that he i did not consider the present fees were too high n small towns, when one bore in mind loss of practice, annoy- ance, repeated visits, and clerical work involved in the performance of the duties. If the fees were reduced he would have to ask for an increase of salary for parish work.

The CLERK said that would be a distinct question. The CHAIRMAN : He is not bound to retain the office of public vaccinator. Dr. PEACOCKE And Dr. BENNETT, the vaccinators for Warrington, were in attendance to place their views before the Guardians.

The CHAIRMAN said the Special Committee gave long consideration to the question, with the assistance of two vaccination officers. They were unanimous in the belief that in deciding to reduce the fees to the sums named they were dealing with the officers in a liberal spirit and that the amounts were quite adequate for the work required. . Mr. MATHER said the Board had every confidence in the ability of the committee to settle the question and he agreed that they had dealt liberally with the doctors. Mr. FURNESS said the reasonable character of the recommendations ought to appeal to every member of the Board. Mr. EVAN'S said the conditio--,s In the scattered rural areas were not quite the same as obtained in the town, but he understood the committee's reccommendations applied all round. In some cases three visits would probably have to be paid to patients and in a scattered district that meant something. The recommendations hardly appeared to be equitable. The CLERK said it was the custom to pay extra remuneration for long distances. He submitted a state- ment of the amounts paid to the public vaccinators in four years, which were as follows :—Dr. Peacocke, £ll3l 9s. ; average £282 19s. 9d. ; Dr. Bennett £l,lll 17s. 6d.; average £277 19 4d; Dr. Dowling, average r £9B 3s. 9d.; Dr. Sephton, average £2B 17s id.; Dr. Valentine total £722 65., average £lBO us. 6d. With regard to what had been done in other Unions, the practice varied. Some Boards had reduced the fees to a minimum all round; some had fixed about the Isame rate as the Warrington committee proposed; and others were paying a little more. A medical man in a town might find a whole day's work in a single street, whereas the country doctor might spend half a day on one case. That was why the committee had fixed 3s. as the amount for Warrington, and 3s. 6d. for rural districts. Of course, in the country there was also a mileage rate which was not'paid in Warrington. Mr. BOLTON asked the Clerk's opinion as to the advis- ability of appointing one doctor to undertake the duties of public vaccinator.

The CHAIRMAN : We cannot think of that. The CLERK said that if the Board desired to make a change of that kind they would have to give a month's notice to all their vaccinators. They had, however, decided not to do that but to reduce the fees which bad been a subject of complaint ever since the Local Government Board order was made.

Mr. FURNE3S said it would appear that at some future time it would be to the interests of the rate- payers to employ a permanent doctor as vaccinator. The Board was paying an average of £B5B a year for vaccination and that sum, he took it, was apart from the allowance of is. per case which the doctow received from the Local Government Board.
The CHAIRMAN said the question of a permanent appointment might be a proper one to consider at some future time, but it was out of order now.
Dr. Peacoolie and Dr. Bennett were than called into the room to lay their views before the Board.

Dr. PEAcocir, submitted a statement on the duties of public vaccinators which, he contended, were very onerous aud responsible, entailing repeated visits and much clerical work. The work was subject to the strict regulation and inspection of the Local Govern- ment Board, and the vaccinators had to incur consider- able out-of-pocket expenses. He submitted that 3s. was inadequate to the great amount of work and responsi- bility entailed in efficient vaccination, and asked the Board to grant at least 3s. 6d. all round. Dr. BENNETT endorsed these views. Mr. BENT : Do I understand that the doctor has four forms to fill up in respect of each case, for the benefit of the Local Government Board? Dr. PEACOCKE : Yes, The CHAIRMAN : The doctor did not supplement his remarks by intimating that he never had to render an account, and always got his money in full. (Laughter). The doctors having retired, Mr. DAVIES said he was rather surprised at the amount of labour involved. It was greater than he had imagined. The CHAIRMAN said Dr. Peacocke had made out a strong case but he (the chairman) was satisfied that the committee were acting in a liberal spirit. Mr. MATHER moved that the committee's recommen- dation be adopted. Mr. RITCHIE seconded.

div.head: FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.
SOME CLOSE CONTESTS.

The annual sports promoted by the Warrington Football Club have long constituted the great August Bank Holiday attraction locally, and the enterprise of I the Club in arranging these admirable meetings has been vs ell supported by the townspeople. AlthOugh on Monday thousands of Warringtonians were induced to take advantage of the delightful weather and betake themselves to holiday resorts, many preferred to stay at home and the sports were well patronised. The turnstiles clicked merrily, and by two o'clock— the hour fixed for the opening of the long prcgramme —there would be an attendance of about 5,000. There was a falling off in the entries,but some excellent races were provided, several noted athletes figuring. The programme embraced 19 events and, thanks t,) the splendid arrangements, the contests were got through most expeditiously. Some exceedingly close finishes were witnessed in the fiat races, the great feature being the 'victories of Jaffir Rumjahn, of Liverpool, who carried off the first prizes in the 100 yards and 220 yards handicaps. This fine young athlete has come over Ifrom India to study medicine at the Liverpool University and promises to achieve notable successes lin the realm of sport. Local competitors were well ito the fore and it was pleasing to note that many prizes went to the Warrington men. J. Houghton is to I be congratulated upon winning the two miles bicycle race after a close struggle and it is worthy of note that all the prizes in the 880 yarcls handicap went to local entrants. The cycle races were carried through almost without spills, and there was no serious hitch to mar any part of the sports. The Borough IBand was in attendance and, under the conductorship lof Mr. Griffin, discoursed lively music. Praise is due Ito the officials for their painstaking efforts to ensure the success of the festival. They were :- 1 Clerk of the course, Mr. T. Davies; starter, Mr. T. Wainwright; judges, Messrs. J. He jumped off in front of another car which was proceeding in the opposite direction awl was knoeked down and so terribly Injured that death took place within a few minutes.

div.head: FACTORY SET ON FIRE.
div.p: FACTORY SET ON FIRE.
Warrington Girl Charged with Arson
At the Warrington Borough Court, on Wednesday before the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) and other magistrates, _

glittle girl named Mary Potts, living in Turner - street, was charged with wilfully and maliciously setting fire to a quantity of fustian and a fustian-cutting frame in the works of the United Velvet Cutters' Association, Limited, Lythgoe's-lane, doing damage to the amount of £B. She pleaded guilty. It appeared that on the night of July 30, a fire was- discovered at the prosecutor's premises in Lythgoe's- lane. The premises had been securely fastened at 6.40 the same night, and had it not been for the prompt detection of the outbreak a serious blaze with great damage, would have resulted. An examination of the room in which the fire occurred disclosed plain traces of paraffin oil and matches, and everything pointed strongly to the outbreak being due to the wilful and malicious act of some person or persons. Inquiries were made by Detective-sergeant Meacock, with the result that the girl was arrested on Tuesday, and from the first she admitted her guilt. The officer elicited the fact that on Sunday evening, July 28, prisoner, Sarah Ann Richardson, aged 12 years, Alice Ratcliffe, aged 13, and several other girls were playing in the vicinity of Tamer-street when prisoner said, "Come, let's set fire to the cutting shop." They went to the premises, but came away again. The next evening prisoner, Richardson, Ratcliffe, and one or two more girls were together about Turner-street when the prisoner, it was alleged, produced 2d. She and. Richardson went together and purchased a pennyworth of paraffin oil at a small shop and some matches at another shop. They took the bottle containing the oil and the matches to the cutting shop and hid them in a shed at the back of the premises. On the date of the fire the girls again went to Lytheoe's-lane, and the prisoner picked up some bricks or stones and broke two windows in the cutting shop. The other girls then ran away. Prisoner according to her own admission, reached through the broken windows, poured the oil on the fustian and frame, set tire to them, and then ran away. The Chief Constable, in asking for a remand for a week, said it would be a charitable thing for the girl if she could be got into a home. Her father was in the workhouse, and prisoner and her mother only left the institution six weeks ago. Since then they had been living as best they could. It would be in the interests Qf all concerned if the girl was sent away. The remand was granted.

WHITE CITY, MANCHESTER. HALE'S TOURS OF THE WORLD. The air of the Sumer Park, like the White City, has a surprising effect on its patrons, there is something jubilant and exhilarating about it, the festivity of the place effects both young ond old. Visitorsare attracted there, not only for the joys afforded them, but for the, , sweet restfulness as well as the interesting tradition. and natural charms found there. This has been fully demonstrated on Bank Holiday, when over 62,000 visitors enjoyed the rest, comfort and enjoyment that this resort affords. The managing director, Mr. J. Calvin Brown, is to be highly complimented on the results, and the directors have been very fortunate in their selection in securing the services of such a com- petent man to superintend the operations of this vast amusement proposition, forhe is the largest factor in the successful operations of the White City. He so modest and unpretentious that it is rare that he gets' into the limelight of publicity, but, as unassuming and retiring as his manner is, the smallest detail never escapes his watchful eye, or those of his alert and trusty lieutenants.

It is true that true art in its most perfect form 19 but an imitation of nature, and, while valuable in a pre- servative character in immortalising, In proportion to the ability of its creator, it can never excel in interest or result the effect that nature unadorned possesses in itself. ThE art connoisseur raves over a painting, not because it is a painting, but because it so nearly resembles nature, and the closer the resemblance the greater the value, as well as the effect. Similarly is this true of the drama, and the opera, no matter how much enthusiasm it creates, analysis compels truth to admit that there is an artificiality. Plays that are founded upon facts and interpreted by great actors, while of immense educative value, cause admiration on account of the skill of the dramatist and personator in proportion to their ability to simulate nature. Shakes- peare and otkers no doult have impressed the history of certain times more effectively upon the public mind, as they give it more vividly and lastingly than the mere recorder of facts, the veracious historian. The historian or the dramatist until lately, has been depend- ent a great deal for his characters and date to legendarY lore handed down from father to son, or to impressions j that have either lost their strength or become exagger- ated by the lapse of time. Not so with Hale's Tours of the world, they hold , the mirror up to nature and are at the same time novel, educational, and entertaining. A trip by one of their tours is always an object lesso

COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER. BYE-LAWS for the good rule and government of the ADMINIS- TRATIVE COUNTY OF CHESTER (excepting the Municipal Boroughs situate therein). NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Cheshire County Council, at a Meeting held at Chester Castle on Thursday, the Ist day of August, 1907, made the following Bye-laws, viz. : TOUTING. No person shall in any street or public place for the purpose of selling or advertising any article or obtaining custom tout or importune to the annoy- ance or obstruction of passengers. SHOOTING GALLERIES, ETC. No person shall in any street or public place or on any land adjoining or near thereto keep or manage or cause to be kept or managed a shooting gallery swingboat rouniabout or any other construction of a like character so as to cause obstruction or danger to the traffic in any such street or public place. DEFACING BUILDINGS WALLS FOOT PAVEMENTS ETC. No person shall except with the consent of the owner or occupier or person having the charge thereof or unless authorised so to do by law deface by writing or other marks any building wall pillar window lamp-post or other post in or abutting on a street or public, place nor shall any person affix any posting bill advertisement or other paper upon the foot pavement in any street or public place or stomp or estenoil VP Ith pant Or ot}sorvrioo any word or figure upon any such pavement. NOISY ANIMALS. No person shall keep within any house building or premises any noisy animal which shall be or cause a serious nuisance to residents in the neighbour- hood. Provided that no proceedings shall be taken against any person for an offence against this Bye- law unless the nuisance be continued after the expiration of a fortnight from the date of the service on such person of a notice alleging a nuis- ance signed by not less than three householders residing within hearing of the animal. THROWING ORANGE PEEL, ETC., ON STREETS. No person shall to the annoyance or danger of passengers throw or deposit in or upon any street or public place in any Urban District orange or lemon peel or the rind of any other fruit or vegetable. INTERPRETATIONS. " Street " means and includes a highway any public bridge and any road lane footpath square quay court alley or passage whether a highway or not to which the public have access. "Public place "includes any common park pleasure ground or roadside waste to which the public have access. PENALTIES. Any person who shall offen3 against any of the fore- going bye-laws shall be liable for each offence to a Penalty not exceeding forty shillings. AND NOTICE IS lIKREBY FURTHER GIVEN, that a sealed copy of min Byelaws has been forwarded to the Secretary of State. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 2nd August, 1907.

_ NOTES AND NOTIONS. The "Palace of Justice" is to be cleaned and decorated apparently, the Borough Surveyor having been instructed to report upon the cost. o The applications for shares in the Warrington Garden Suburbs Co. have been of an encouraginc, nature, but the whole of the requisite capital is not encouraging subscribed. Investors with a desire to forward so praiseworthy a scheme are requested to make early application for shares. We are glad to hear that the London and North- Western Railway Company propose to strengthen and partly re-construct the old iron railway bridge at Arpley. It has often occurred to us that the bridge was not a particularly safe-looking structure, and there would be the makings of a very nasty accident if, at any time, it collapsed. * * * It must have been a sad blow to the men of the Ist V.B. South Lancashire Regiment at Llanberis to learn that their late popular Colonel was no more. In Colonel Ridgway every ranker had a friend, and the whole- hearted work and enthusiasm of the deceased gentle- man is reflected in the morale and strength of the local volunteer battalion. 000 With the view of preventing too much black smoke issuing from factory chimneys an ingenious device is finding favour in Blackburn. By means of a curiously-shaped mirror in the boiler shed the fireman has the summit of the tall chimney brought within his view. Thus he knows when he.is close to violat- ing the law. A large supply of these mirrors is wanted in Warrington. • * * * Another public bowling green is not only being mooted, but is taking practical shape. The Town • Hall and Parks Committee has been slow to move, but at last it has done so —slightly. A request has been sent to the Finance Committee for the use of the plot of land behind Garven Place, Sankey-street, as a public bowling green. What the Finance Committee thinks of the idea we shall probably hear at Tuesday's Council meeting. . .

Congregationalism has lost its oldest church member through the death of Mrs. ‘Venham in her 103rd year, at Highgate. Mrs. Wenham had latterly been unable to attend public worship, but she took an active interest in its affairs, and for some years past the deacons of the church had presented her with a bouquet on her birthday. RAILWAY PORTER ELECTROCUTED. A shocking death by electricity befel a porter at Harrow Station on the Metropolitan Railway on Tues- day. He was coupling up two carriages, when one of his feet became wedged between two rails, and in attempting to extricate the limb he fell with his face on the "live " rail. Fie was instantly electrocuted his boots being burned through and his face terribly scorched.
